That was the whole shape of her life since the Cataclysm: every justification she built was true, and every true thing she built it over was a body.

She was counting the stones for the fifth time — still one hundred thirty-nine or one hundred forty, depending on whether the half-hidden stone counted — when Thistle's face arrived.

Not like a memory summoned. Like a fish surfacing in still water, a rise, a ring of light. The service gate of the Founders' Quarter: iron bars flaking with rust where the gardeners' damp had reached them, a wicket cut into the larger door for the passage of small things — baskets, letters, hands. Vex had been standing in the lane, the heat a low coal in her palms, trying to look smaller than she was, hoping for water or work or any kindness the Founders' kitchens might set loose. Too angry to beg, too hungry to refuse. Then the wicket opened and a face looked out at her: a girl's face, younger than her own, sharp-chinned, with eyes too old for the smoothness of her skin and a cap holding back hair that had long given up on staying tamed. The girl studied her for a long moment. Vex studied back. The lane was quiet around them — the sound of horses somewhere distant, the smell of slops and cut flowers tangled together.

"Huh," said the girl, and laughed.

It was a sharp, crooked sound, like a stone skipped across water, like a door opening on the bright side of a bad day. It was not a kind laugh. It was a laughing-at laugh, amused and appraising, and Vex felt hot blood rise in her face. Then the heel of a loaf came through the wicket — flour-dusted, still faintly warm — dropped without ceremony into Vex's hands. The girl's hands were pale from washing, chapped at the knuckles, and she wiped them on her apron before she made the shooing gesture.

"Don't tell them," she said. "And don't make me sorry."

That was the whole first meeting. No name exchanged. Vex learned it weeks later, learned to say it in her head like a coin she kept turning over: *Thistle.* The bread had been warm. The girl had been laughing at her. And yet the memory had a sweetness in it she could not dig out, a sweetness that hurt more than any of the ledger's cruelties. Because Thistle had been alive. Because she had chosen to open the wicket, to look at a stranger in a lane, to throw bread at her, to laugh. Because in the dark of the tear-shaped cell the memory was not a reproach and not a comfort — it was simply a fact. There had been a girl with a sharp laugh, and the fire had taken her, and Vex had been the one who lit it.

The memory stayed with her through the long hollow of the night, grew bars and a gate and a lane that went somewhere it should not have gone. She must have fallen asleep against the wall, huddled where the stranger's tallies stood — because suddenly she was back at the service gate, except it was wrong. The lane was full of smoke. The wicket was open and Thistle was on the other side of it, reaching through, her mouth open on a word the fire drowned. Vex tried to call out to warn her, tried to run to her, tried to reach the gate — but her hands were the fire, the fire was her hands, and the lane and the iron and the girl's face were all going up in the same bright roar.

She woke screaming. The scream came from the bottom of her the way the fire itself had come on the night of the Cataclysm — not chosen, not controlled, a column of sound that hit the stones and shattered. No one was there to hear it but the damp and the rat-shaped shadows and the fifty-three tallies of the dead stranger. She screamed until her throat tore, and then, because her mouth was no longer enough, she clawed the wall.

She scraped her nails across the stone, dragging downward, digging for purchase — for some solid grip on a world outside her own skull. The stone was wet and unforgiving. The first pass peeled skin from her knuckles. She did it again, and again, raking her hands down the courses until her nails tore and her palms left red smears over the stranger's honest notches. The pain was a fact. The pain was something she could hold. The cell swam back into focus around her: the tear-shape of it, the dome above, the grate with its merciless slant of light. Her breath came ragged. Her hands throbbed. The blood on the stone was real in a way the ledger was not, and the ledger in her head was real in a way the stones were not. Nothing connected. Everything connected. She pressed her forehead to the wet rock and forced herself to breathe, slower, slower, until the panic loosened its grip on her throat.

Thistle was dead. That was the fact beneath all the other facts. Thistle was dead, and Vex was alive, and the city was grateful in the dark and hungry in the light. No ledger of the Founders' crimes would ever make the sum come out clean. She could spend the short remainder of her life counting stones and reciting her mother's prayers and building cases in her head. It would not put the water back in Marnie's veins. It would not put the smile back on Thistle's face. It would not unburn the white dress.

She said the names aloud, because the cell needed to hear them, because she was the keeper of the truth now and the truth had faces. "Marnie. Thistle." Her voice came out in shreds. She pressed her bleeding hands flat against the stone, the way she had once pressed them against the Founders' gate, and held them there until the wet rock drank the warmth of her palms.

That was when she heard it.

Behind the wall. Under the slow drip of moisture and the distant bell: a sound like a nail drawn across stone. Not a rat — the rats had their own particular scratch, scuttling and quick. This was slower. Deliberate. A sound with intention in it.

Vex froze. The scraping stopped. The dark closed in, listening too.

She waited so long that her hands went numb against the stone. She was on the point of deciding she had imagined it — that she had finally scraped the edge off her own mind, that the screaming had loosened something in her that should have stayed knotted — when it came again. One scratch. Then two, on the other side. Then silence, patient as an answer.

Something behind the wall was scratching back.

chapters.name: The Split Self
chapters.content:
She wakes with the sea in her ears.

It was a good dream—the kind that leaves salt on the skin. Gray water to the far edge of the world, the long breath of a tide coming in, Thistle standing at the shore with her hair escaping its cap, saying *I told you. I told you it was real.* Vex believed her for whole seconds, longer than she has believed anything since Marnie died. Then the drip of the cell breaks through—old iron, wet stone, the dark—and the sea runs out of her like water from fingers that try too late to cup it. The cell returns in its usual order: the weeping curve of the wall, the grate's pale coin of light, the bread Wyman left in its rope basket. Untouched. She cannot remember deciding not to eat.

A thought arrives in a voice she knows too well. She has taken to calling it, and its counterpart, the two guards of her cell, posted on the inside of the walls: the Arsonist, who walked her to the gate, and the Penitent, who keeps the list of the dead.

*Your body is a loyal animal,* the Arsonist observes. *It wants what it wants. It does not care about your scruples. Eat the bread. Drink the water. Live to see history written.*

"History," Vex says to the stones. Her voice comes out a stranger's, rusty from disuse.

*You survived a fire that spared no one else. Does that mean nothing to you?*

"It means I'm the one who lit it."

A softer voice answers—worse, because it does not argue so much as remember. *The laundress,* the Penitent says. *The one whose name you never knew. She washed Founders' sheets to feed her children. You passed her at the well on your way to the gates. You saw the smudge of ash on her wrist where the pump handle marked her. You saw the children's shoes tied by the laces over her shoulder, swinging with her step. Did you remember them, Vex, while the fire took the kitchens? Did you think about the feet that would have worn them?*

Vex presses her palms to her eyes. The crescents bite her cheekbones.

*You deserve the pyre,* the Penitent says, without anger, the way the ceiling drips. *Every flame of it. That is the only history you will have.*

The two of them have circled each other for days, dogs around a bone. This is the first time they have both spoken her name.

*Marnie was breathless on the bed,* the Arsonist says, cold as a court clerk. *The healer's door was shut in your face. The banquet menu hung on the public board while your sister died of thirst—quail in honey, wine-glazed pheasant, cream served in cups of cistern ice. You saw it. Everyone saw it. Name the punishment that balances that crime. There is only one. You found it. You held it in your hands, and you opened your hands where the locks were.*

"The fire took the kitchens first," Vex says into her palms. "It took people who had never turned a lock on a cistern in their lives."

*Collateral.* The word is clean, polished, businesslike. *Every war has it. History forgives the sack of a city its brothels; it will forgive you the kitchens and note the Founders' hoard, and move on. You opened the granaries. You opened the cisterns. Children drink in the lower districts because of what you did.*

*And whose kitchens were they?* the Arsonist asks, softer now, and therefore worse. *The Founders' kitchens. The same kitchens that posted the menu and counted the ration. The girl who served at that table—you knew her. The scullery maid with the sharp laugh, who stole a heel of bread and threw it over the wall as if that made her one of yours. She ate their leavings. She smiled at their plates. She stayed.*

"The bread was warm," Vex says. "She gave it through the gate. She did not own the gate. She did not own the lock."

*She stayed.*

"She was a girl. There was nowhere else for her to go."

*She chose the Founders' roof. You chose the fire. You are both choosers. History will note that she chose to fatten on scraps, and that the scraps stopped coming when the fire ate the kitchen.*

Thistle's laugh arrives—not the dream, the real one. Sharp and crooked, like a stone skipped across water. Vex has carried it for weeks without letting it argue. Now she lets it.

*She wanted to see the sea,* the Penitent says. *She told me she would show it to me. She was the only person in the city who believed I would ever be anywhere else. And the fire ate her first, before it ever reached the locks. That is not justice. That is the beast you fed. You fed it her.*

"Is that what you told yourself at the gate?" Vex asks. "Or did you tell yourself the fire would know the innocent?"

Silence. That is the Penitent's sharpest cut—the question the Arsonist cannot answer without hanging herself. Because Vex remembers the gate. The heat gathering in her palms, the smell of her own skin about to give, the certainty rising in her chest like a second flame: the fire would be surgical. It would burn the locks, the doors, the banquet table. It would walk past the servants' block with its eyes fixed on the guilty. It would not touch a single person who had ever only been hungry. She believed it the way you believe a promise—a promise no one made her. She made it herself, to herself.

She opened her hands. Fire does what fire does. It eats.

*You knew,* the Penitent says. *In the walk. At the gate. You knew you could not fully control it. You told yourself so, and then you uncurled your fingers anyway. That is the whole fact. Everything else is the Arsonist, decorating the walls.*

Vex goes to her knees at the floor's narrow point—the point of the tear—and presses her forehead to the wet stone. The mineral taste of the place comes up through her teeth. She has no argument. That is the unbearable thing: both voices are true, and the two truths do not fit in one body. The Arsonist holds Marnie's blue lips and the open cisterns and the city's nighttime whisper of thanks, and says: justice has a shape, and you gave it shape. The Penitent holds the laundress's swinging shoes and the Foundling child's white dress and Thistle's crooked laugh, and says: you could have walked away. You could have found another way if you had wanted one. You did not want one. You wanted to burn.

There it is. The two mouths of the split, and the truth standing between them, nameless, patient, horrible.

She tries the middle ground. *It was justice with a flaw in it.* The flaw is the size of a city quarter. She tries *it was grief that got hold of a weapon.* The grief was hers; she made a torch of it and called it a verdict. The middle ground does not hold her. It is ground—a place to stand while pretending she did not walk to the gate with open hands and a lit furnace where her heart should have been. Both selves, she sees, are escapes with the same door: they make the fire mean something other than her.

*What are you running from?* she asks, in a voice that belongs to neither of them.

The drip. The cold. The bread in its basket, going soft against the weave—the kind her mother made only for festival days. She stares until her eyes blur and thinks the way she thought once before, in the floury dark of the bakery, with the ache of the forbidden heat in her palms. She learned then what the fire is: will. It answered her small desires. The candle she never touched. The flour sack, after the apprentice's cruelty, gone up in a pulse of white and gold before her mother could scream. A will can be greedy. A will can want more than the hand that holds it can spend.

At the gate she willed the fire to break the locks. She did not will it to stop. And in the first shout of alarm from the Founders' Quarter, the first crack of a beam giving where she had not sent it—she felt triumph. She told herself that afterward. Horror came so fast behind it that she never looked at the triumph; she let the Penitent bury it.

The truest thing she felt that night was pleasure.

The word arrives like a spark finding dry grass. Vex goes still. The cold of the stone digs into her knees, and under it, under the fear and the shame she wears like the cell's own clothing, there it is, warm as a banked coal: the first minute of the Cataclysm felt good. The roar was a voice saying everything she had never been allowed to say. The Founders' festival music stopped. The great gates, unmoved by a hundred petitions, began to groan. And a scorched small thing inside her—the part that carried Marnie's coffin with the iron paws for handles—opened its mouth and drank the first scream from the Quarter like the first water after a month of thirst. She wanted it. Not justice. Not the opened cisterns, not the city's salvation. The wanting was simpler, older, more her own than any of the words she has wrapped around it since. She wanted them to be afraid. She wanted them to feel what a locked cistern feels like from the outside. She wanted to be the hand that did it, and for one minute of her life the whole city knew her name and feared it. That is what she has been running from, lying in the dark and letting the two guards tear her between them like a loaf: she has been trying not to remember that she loved the burning, for one minute, before it grew teeth.

The heat wakes in her palms. Not the low banked coal she has carried through her weeks in the cell—something yellow and reaching, running up her forearms like a hand hunting for a throat. The crescent scars gleam faintly, then white.

Vex shoves her hands under her armpits and clamps her elbows to her sides, grinding her palms into her ribs. Stop. *Stop.* She grabs the heat the way a net grabs a hare, finds it, smothers it—forces it back down her arms, down into the furnace of her chest where she has kept it caged since the trial. It resists. It has smelled the want. It *is* the want. She wrestles it, breathing through locked teeth, horrified at what she is holding down, at the fact that it still lives in her, that it rises whenever the want rises, until the glow dies in the seams of her fists. Then she lies on the cold stone, arms pinned beneath her, forehead on the floor, shaking.

*It is still there,* the Arsonist says, amused, from somewhere above her. *It will always be there. You can starve it. You can chain it. You can call it monstrous. It was born in you. It is you.*

*Then I will die,* Vex thinks. *I will die on their pyre and take it with me.*

The Penitent is silent. For a moment she believes it is satisfied. Then the Penitent speaks in the tone of the memory—not the Foundling child's voice, the voice it does not have, but the tone of the moment itself: the small white figure on the brick balcony, the eyes meeting hers across the heat. *You will. And it will be a mercy to die and take it with you. But you do not get to choose the manner. You get the pyre, Vex. You get to feel fire from the other side. That is what you made. That is all you ever made.*

The day passes. There is no other way to measure it. The light crawls along the weep-dark stone, finger by finger, from west to east, and Vex lies where the Penitent left her, at the tear's point, arms still pressed against her chest, hunger arriving like a tide and receding, thirst after it. She does not rise. She does not touch the bread. Through the grate she hears the city's ordinary life going on without her—the bread-seller's bell at the sixth hour, the crier's hoarse call, a burst of laughter that cuts off as someone remembers what is underneath. Wyman's step comes and goes above her—the drag of the left boot, the pause, the bolt, the grate scraping back—and the basket stays full. She cannot tell him why. She cannot explain that she has stopped being sure there is a her left to feed. The two voices argue in the corridor of her skull without her, a noise now—names and ledgers and the white dress and the open cisterns—all of it said, all of it to be said again. She is not the rope anymore. She is the gap the rope has been drawn through.

At some point she finds herself at the wall, her fingers on the stranger's notches—the fifty-three tally marks blurred with the blood she left there on the night of the Thistle dream. She stopped adding to them. Perhaps whoever cut them also stopped, one night, and left the rest of their time unmarked. She runs her thumb across the soft, damp edges and tries to think of some use for the knowledge. There is none. The hours stack themselves. She tries her mother's prayer and hears it in the Arsonist's voice—*Flame of Order, chasten her hands. Make her clay, not coal*—and the prayer does not take. She was never clay. The fog comes up out of the stone and fills her.

In the last of the light Wyman comes again. The grate scrapes. "You didn't eat," he says, from a long way off. Bread is replaced in the basket, the water skin refilled. A pause. "The pyre's building in the square. They'll come for you when it's ready." Another pause, longer. "You'd best decide which one of you is going to stand on it."

She wants to tell him she is trying. The words will not assemble. The grate closes, his steps drag away, the light leaves the wall, and the bell rings the dark in.

The scratching begins at the deepest hour, when the two voices have worn each other out and the cell's silence is full of their footprints. Behind the wall it goes: one, then two, then a pause, then one. Patient as a question. She lies in the dark with the bread beside her and the water skin hanging from its rope, and does not answer it. She has no voice that is not two voices. She has no self to scrape against the stone.

The night is deep and almost peaceful, like the inside of a held breath. Somewhere above her the city sleeps. Somewhere behind the wall the scratch waits. She lies between them—alive, emptied, no longer two, not yet one—and lets the night hold her. The waiting, she understands, with the last clear part of her mind, is the only answer she has left to give. Not to the thing behind the wall. To herself. It is enough, for now, to be the one asking the question; perhaps that is the whole of what she has left—a woman who has stopped believing both her selves and cannot yet find a third. The morning will bring the light, and the light will bring the two voices back, and she will lie between them as she has lain all day: empty, exhausted, alive. It is not a place to stand. But it is hers.

chapters.name: The Scullery Maid's Smile
chapters.content:
The cell has learned her breathing. It rises and falls with her, the drip keeping time like a pulse inside the stone, and when she sleeps she cannot tell whether she sleeps or merely stops defending. The bread sits where Wyman left it. She has watched it go from soft to stiff, the flour-dust settling into the weave of the cloth, the crust developing a pale geography of cracks. She has watched it the way a prisoner watches a window—as though if she looks long enough, it will open.

She is burning. Not the fire—the fever. It crawls up from her empty stomach, lights in her joints, makes the stone wall ripple when she looks at it. She pressed her forehead to the wet rock and the rock drank her heat and gave it back as cold. Her hands shake. She has not eaten in—she counts the light shafts—two days. Three. She loses count in the middle of counting, and the losing feels like a kind of falling, like dropping a stitch she will not be able to pick back up.

The drip becomes a footstep. The footstep becomes a laugh.

She is not in the cell.

---

The gate. Rust-flaking iron bars, a wicket cut at waist height for small things—bread, notes, coins, charity that does not want to look at the hands reaching for it. Vex is fourteen, thin in the way of the lower districts, and she has been standing at the service gate for the better part of an hour, hoping a servant will come out with slops. Her apron is clean but her hands are flour-bleached from the morning's kneading, and her mother's voice is still in her ears—*stay small, pray, come straight home*—but the bread ran out two days ago, and Marnie was hungry this morning, and Marnie's hunger is a bell that does not stop ringing.

On the other side of the bars, a courtyard paved in stone that has never known mud. On her side, a lane that floods when it rains and smells of the tannery, a rut worn deep where the service carts come and go. She has learned the rhythm of the gate: the cook's boy at dawn, the laundry women at mid-morning, the scullery staff after the noon meal. She is late for the noon slot. She knows it. She lingers anyway.

A shadow falls across the wicket. A girl peers through—sharp-chinned, cap failing against a spill of dark hair, eyes too old for her face. She studies Vex a long moment, head cocked, weighing something. There is no pity in the look. Pity, Vex has learned, is a kind of wall. This is something else—assessment, curiosity, the frank stare of someone who has decided that looking at a thing directly is the only honest way to see it.

"Huh," the girl says.

Then she laughs. Quick, crooked, a stone skipped across water. A laughing-at laugh—not cruel, but not soft either. She has seen the begging stance before, the shoulder cocked, the hands held out to show they are empty, and she is not fooled by it. She has begged herself, perhaps. She knows the shape of it from the inside.

"Don't tell them," the girl says, and drops a heel of bread through the wicket—warm, flour-dusted, the crust still crackling, the kind of bread Vex's mother made only for Founders' festivals. "And don't make me sorry."

The bread lands in Vex's hands. The warmth of it is obscene, a small burning sun in her palms. The girl is already turning away, the cap falling over one eye, and Vex says—later she will not remember deciding to say it—"I won't."

The girl glances back. Smiles. Quick, crooked, defiant. The smile of someone who has decided something and will not be talked out of it. The smile of someone who knows she is stealing from the Founders' own table and does not care what the Founders would think.

Then she is gone, and the gate is bars again, and Vex stands in the lane holding a warmth she did not think existed anywhere inside the walls of the Founders' Quarter.

---

Weeks later. Thistle comes to the wicket with a bucket of peelings, sets it down, and immediately begins to mimic someone—this is her habit, the way other people breathe. She draws herself up, pulls her cap down to her eyebrows, and speaks in a voice pitched exactly like a Founder's, round and slow and complacent: "The poor are the Order's garden. We water them with patience and weed them with providence."

Vex laughs so hard she snorts. Thistle's grin flashes—that crooked flash—and she goes on, warming to her audience: "And remember, children, hunger is a trial. Starvation is character-building. Thirst is simply the body's way of praying."

She is the Head of the Water Board now, striding the cobbles of the service yard with an imaginary cane. She coughs, or rather performs a cough, the kind of cough that is really a declaration of importance. "I have drunk from every cistern in the Quarter and found them all excellent." She pretends to sip from an invisible cup, holds it to the light, examines it with the fastidious disgust of a woman tasting vinegar and calling it wine. Then she spits. "Tastes like the lower districts. Needs more honey."

They laugh until they are breathless, crouched on either side of the gate, and Vex thinks—she will remember this thought later, turning it like a coin—that this is the most alive she has ever felt. The girl on the other side of the iron has a gift for making the unbearable bearable by making it absurd. She has taken the thing that crushes them and turned it into a puppet, and for the length of the performance, the puppet is the one in the cage.

But there is a blade under the mockery. Thistle's eyes, when she stops laughing, are not amused. She leans against the bars, close enough that Vex can see the chapped line of her mouth, the flush of exertion on her cheeks.

"They think we're patient," Thistle says quietly. "They think we're grateful. They think the Order is right—that suffering is a test, and that we pass it by dying quietly." She picks up a stray stone from the yard, weighs it in her hand. "I'd like to see the Founders feel it. Just once. Just one day of the ration line. One hour watching their children's lips go blue." She drops the stone. It clatters on the cobbles. "Then they'd understand."

Vex says nothing. She cannot say what she is thinking: that she has imagined the same thing, but with fire. That sometimes she lies awake and feels the heat gathering in her palms and imagines the Founders' gates groaning, the cisterns cracking open, water running free in the streets. She has never told anyone this. She has never told anyone what her hands can do. The secret sits in her chest like a second heart, and when Thistle says *then they'd understand*, the heart beats faster.

Thistle smiles again, quick and crooked and defiant, and Vex understands that the smile is not a joke. It is a promise. Against the locked cisterns and the posted menus and the healer's shut door, Thistle's smile is a small, burning refusal: *you will not make me small.*

Vex wants to tell her. She wants to say: *I am not small. I carry a fire that does not burn me. I could open their gates with my bare hands.* The words gather in her throat like cinders.

She says: "I like your laugh."

Thistle laughs—the real one, quick and crooked—and the moment passes.

---

Night. Vex has slipped out after closing, meeting Thistle in the lane behind the fish-monger's—a loophole in the curfew, a small rebellion of its own. The lane smells of brine and scales and the particular damp of a place that has held too many things that were once alive. They sit on the steps, wrapped in the same blanket Vex stole from her mother's trunk, and Thistle talks about the sea.

"I saw it in a book once," Thistle says. "The steward—he had a book with pictures. I was scrubbing the floor and I saw it, open on his desk." Her voice goes low, awed. "It was gray, the whole world gray, and it moved. It was alive."

Vex tries to imagine it. Meridian has no sea. It has the cisterns, the wells, the rationed buckets; rain that is never enough, water that tastes of iron and coin. The sea is a rumor, a heresy, a word the Order does not say. Water that does not answer to a Founder is a contradiction, a thing that cannot exist inside the walls of the world she knows.

"It moves," Thistle repeats. "All the time. It does not stop. It does not ask permission. Can you imagine—water that has no gate, no key, no name on a deed? Water that just *is*?"

Vex shakes her head. She cannot. The idea is too large for her to hold.

"Water falls from the sky there," Thistle whispers. "Not rationed. Not metered. It just falls, and everyone drinks, and no one asks whose name is on the cistern." She is looking past the rooftops, past the city, at something Vex cannot see. "I'm going to see it someday. I'm going to stand at the edge and put my hands in it and it will be warm and it will not be counted out to me."

Her voice catches. Even in the dark, Vex can see her face.

"I'm going to see the sea," Thistle says, "and I'm going to laugh, and no one is going to tell me to be quiet."

Vex says nothing. *I will go with you,* she thinks. *I will keep you safe. I will burn anything that tries to stop you, and I will burn it down to ash.*

She does not say it. She is not good at saying things. She reaches across the blanket and takes Thistle's hand, and they sit in the dark, two girls under a curfew, dreaming of water that falls freely.

Thistle's smile, in the dark, is quick and crooked and defiant.

It is the last time Vex sees her whole.

---

Fever.

Drip. Stone. The cell.

Vex comes to with her cheek against the wet rock and the memory draining out of her like water from fingers that try too late to cup it. She is shaking. The fever has her in its teeth. She presses her palms to the stone and the crescents throb—the marks, the seams where the fire comes out.

She tries to burn the memory away.

She reaches into her chest and finds the heat, coiling, patient, her own pulse made visible. She feeds it the memory—the smile, the bread, the whisper of the sea—and the fire rises in her hands, yellow, hungry, and she thrusts it at the wall, at the dark, at the place in her mind where Thistle lives.

The fire does nothing. It licks the stone, paints the dark with a brief, greedy light, and gutters out in her palms, leaving only the crescents gleaming white. The memory is untouched. The smile is still there, quick and crooked and defiant, a splinter under her skin that will not work itself out.

She tries again. The fire rises, lower this time, weaker—her body is eating itself now, and there is nothing left to feed it. She drives it at Thistle, at the bread-warmth, at the smell of the sea, and the fire fails, and the memory remains.

"You cannot burn it," she says aloud. The words scrape her throat like gravel. "You cannot burn the only warm thing you ever had."

Because that is the truth, and the truth is the splinter. Thistle was not a casualty. Thistle was not collateral damage, a number on a clerk's list, a household struck from a registry. Thistle was the girl who gave her bread when the Order said to starve. Thistle was the girl who made her laugh in the shadow of the locked cisterns. Thistle was the girl who dreamed of the sea, who wanted only for the Founders to feel the hunger they inflicted—not to burn, not to die, just to feel it once. To understand. To look at the ration line and see their children in it.

Thistle had believed that understanding would change them. She had believed that cruelty was a kind of blindness, and that if the Founders could see, they would stop.

Vex gave her an inferno. Vex burned her on an altar of justice Thistle had never asked anyone to build.

She tries the arithmetic. The ledger voice assembles itself in her head, a clerk's dry pen: *Item: the north cisterns, locked since before her birth. Item: the water tax, tripled in a season. Item: the seven-course banquet menu, posted beside the ration notices. Item: the healer's door, shut at dusk. Item: Marnie's blue lips.*

*Item: Thistle.*

She cannot make it balance. There is no sum of Founders' crimes that equals the feel of Thistle's hand in hers, the whisper of the sea, the crooked smile. Every justification she builds is true, and every true thing she builds it over is a body. The ledger will not close. Thistle does not fit in any arithmetic that makes the fire bearable.

And under the arithmetic, a deeper truth: she had known. At the gate, with the heat gathering in her palms, she had known she could not fully control what she was about to release. She had told herself the fire would be surgical, that it would walk past the servants' block with its eyes fixed on the guilty. A promise no one made her. She made it herself, to herself. And then she uncurled her fingers anyway.

She understands, in the fever, what Thistle had actually asked for—not fire, never fire. Thistle wanted the Founders to feel what they had made. She wanted their children's lips to turn blue for a single hour, wanted them to stand in the ration line and watch the posted menu and know the taste of that contempt. It was not a wish for destruction. It was a wish for the world to be less cruel. And Vex—who loved her, who would have died for her, who had thought of her as the warmest thing in her life—had answered that wish with an inferno.

"Thistle," she says. The name is a stone in her mouth. "Thistle, I am sorry."

The cell absorbs it. The drip keeps time. The bread sits, untouched, on the cloth, and the fever wraps her in its arms, and she lets it.

---

As she lies at the tear's point, drifting down into the dark between waking and sleeping, it comes again—behind the wall, below the moss, a sound with intention in it. One scratch, then two, then a pause, then one. Patient as a question.

She has no answer. She has never had an answer. The only thing she had to give anyone was fire, and she gave it, and it ate the girl who dreamed of the sea.

She closes her eyes. The smile waits for her in the dark—quick, crooked, defiant—and she looks at it, and she does not try to burn it, and she lets it see her.

The splinter will not stop digging. That is its mercy. That is its cruelty. That is the only honest thing she has left.

chapters.name: The White Dress
chapters.content:
The scratching has stopped. It stopped when she opened her mouth to answer it, or perhaps it stopped a moment before—she cannot say which came first, only that she lies with her lips parted on a word that was never a name, and the cell's drip keeps time like a pulse inside the stone. The fever is reading her like a book it intends to finish. Every time she closes her eyes she sees the same page.

A child in a white dress. The fever takes her there, and she does not have the strength to refuse.

The night of the founding festival. The Founders' Quarter in firelight. She had come through the gates she had meant to crack, telling herself they would open like a verdict, and the fire had gone ahead of her—faster than her intent, into arcades and courtyards, through silk and waxed beams, through the pink blossoms of the ornamental trees that had never borne fruit, past the fountain that ran day and night for the sound of it. She was not walking into the fire. She was walking after it, shouting. She does not remember what she shouted. Probably *stop*. Probably her sister's name. Probably nothing at all, only a raw sound, a scraped throat, the noise of a creature trying to speak to its own teeth.

The second courtyard had the famous fountain. The water had not been touched. It flung the flames back at itself, broken gold on broken water, so that the whole courtyard seemed to burn twice. The festival tables had been overturned in the flight out. A cup of cistern ice lay on its side, spilling clean water onto the stones while the fire lapped around it. A slaughtered goose lay on the pavers, feathers smoldering, its neck bent at an angle that made Vex's stomach turn. And above the fountain, on a balcony of old brick, she saw the child.

Nine years old. The High Justiciar's daughter. Born on the anniversary of the city's founding—this was her night, her festival, and the white dress was a birthday dress, for the feast, for the seven courses and the cream served in cups of cistern ice. The dress had lace at the collar and a sash of pale gold. A child's dress. A dress that had taken someone's careful fingers a long time to sew. The child had come out to see the commotion, the way children go to a window for lightning. She stood at the balcony rail with both hands on the brick, leaning forward, watching the woman made of flame walk through her burning home.

And their eyes met.

One heartbeat. Vex has spent every night since trying to decide which of them that heartbeat belonged to longer. The child was not screaming. In the instant their eyes met, the child was not screaming. Her mouth was open, but the sound had not caught up with her; her face in the firelight was the face of a child watching something she did not understand. Not terror yet. Not grief. Only the first white shock of a world unmade.

Vex opened her mouth. She meant to say *run—get back inside—you are nine years old, none of this is yours*. She does not know if the word came out. She believes she shouted something. She may have only mouthed it. The heat was in her throat like a second tongue, and the roar of the fire was in her ears, and between the two she could not have heard her own voice if she had tried. But she knows she made the shape of the words. She knows she reached out with one burning hand toward the balcony, as if she could catch the child before she fell.

The blaze came over the balcony rail behind the child like an animal climbing, white at the edges, gold at the throat, and took the white dress. The dress glowed. It is the only word she has for it: the dress glowed, a brief and furious brightness, and then the child was the same color as everything else. The balcony rail was a line of black against the light for a moment, and then it was not. There was a sound—there must have been a sound—but Vex did not hear it. The fire had become a single note, deep in her bones, and the note pitched upward until it eclipsed everything.

She did not fall. She did not run. One heartbeat she was there, and then she was not. The balcony was empty. The rail was gone. The fat pigeons that had roosted in the eaves had burst upward in a panic of burning wings, and the child was not among them. Vex was still screaming at the fire to stop. She does not know how long. The fire did not know her voice. It had never known her voice. It had never known anything but its own hunger, and it went on eating the festival—the white cloths, the wine-glazed pheasant, the cream in its cups of ice—while she stood in the courtyard with the fountain throwing her own fire back at her.

She knelt at the center of the fountain's music, unburned. The fire would not touch her. That was the horror of it, then and now: the beast that ate the child would not eat her. It devoured the festival and the servants' block and Thistle's crooked smile, but it stepped around her like a river around a stone, and left her in the one clean circle of a burning world. She has tried to make that mean something. She was spared to witness. She was spared to be punished. The fire was hers and so the fire would not take her. All of it is true. None of it helps. The beast ate the child and not her. That is the fact. She does not know why it withheld her, except that the appetite had a shape, and her shape was not the one it wanted. It wanted to feed.

The fever loosens its grip for a moment—long enough for the Arsonist to clear its throat. The Arsonist always has a ledger.

Item: the High Justiciar signed the order locking the north cisterns. Item: his name is on the water contracts, on the compact that called hoarding stewardship. Item: the child was born into the Founders' Quarter, raised on bread the poor could not afford, schooled in the doctrine that called starvation a trial and locked gates providence. Nine years old, yes. But nine years old in that house was nine years at the dinner table, nine years of watching her father's key turn in the lock, nine years of learning that the lower districts were a garden to be watered with patience. She would have grown into the key. She would have signed the orders. She would have worn her father's face over her own.

Item: she would have become a tyrant.

Vex tries to hold the item. She reaches for it the way a starving woman reaches for bread in a dream. She would have signed the orders. She would have locked the cisterns. She would have let the children die with blue lips and called it providence and slept well in a clean bed. The arithmetic is sound. Every item is true. That is the terrible thing about the Arsonist: it never lies. It only selects. Like the trial. Like the widow's testimony, true as far as it went, and as far as it went was exactly far enough to put Vex in the oubliette. Even the father's grief had selected: he had testified his daughter as library, archive, palace, never the water, never the cisterns, never the locks.

The memory resists.

It does not argue. That is its cruelty. It simply shows her the child again—the small figure on the brick balcony, both hands on the rail, hands that had never held a key, that had held nothing but bread and a doll and the rail. The white dress glowing. The open mouth. The first white shock of a world unmade. The memory does not show her what the child would have become. It shows her what the child was: nine, small, unarmed, born on a night she did not choose. The fire did not ask her father's name. The fire did not read the ledgers. It did not weigh items. It ate her because she was there.

The fire did not discriminate.

So the Arsonist's column closes itself, every item true and none of them enough, and the balance still reads in the same hand: one white dress. One open mouth. One heartbeat that belonged to her. The fever burns the Arsonist's voice away like pages. She tries to rebuild the item column from the beginning—north cisterns, water tax, the healer's shut door—and the words slide off the memory. The balcony will not be balanced. The child will not be itemized. The beast will not be reasoned with.

And that is the whole truth beneath the Arsonist's careful column: the fire was never a surgical tool. It was a beast. She had told herself it would walk past the servants' block with its eyes on the guilty. She had told herself it would find the keys and open the gates and leave the innocent untouched. She had told herself it could be aimed. It could not. It never had eyes. It had appetite. And the appetite was hers—the pleasure she had taken in the first minute of the burning, the roar, the festival music stopping, the gates groaning. She had fed it. She had opened the cage. The beast was hers, and the beast had its own hunger, and the beast ate a child in a white dress, and the child will never be anything else.

The justification breaks apart. It does not break loudly. It goes the way of all dead arithmetic—silence, then the drip, then the pulse of the stone.

In the present, in the cell, in the sweat and the fever, Vex prays. It is the first time she has meant it. She prays to the Chastened Flame, the Order's god of iron cages and sanctioned candles, the god that would not look at her at her trial. She does not pray for forgiveness. Forgiveness would require a voice on the other end of the prayer, and the child has no voice. She does not pray for the strength to bear the pyre. She prays for the one thing that would make the burning bearable. She prays for the ability to forget.

She uses her mother's words, because they are the only words she has. *Flame of Order, chasten her hands. Let her burn only what she is given. Make her clay, not coal. Make her small. Make her safe.* Then her own words, after: take it from me. Take the dress. Take the balcony. Take the moment of eye contact. Let me die tomorrow and not have to see her while I die.

She says the words aloud. The cell drinks them. The drip keeps time. Her hands lie flat on the stone, crescents turned down, and she keeps them open so the prayer can leave through them, the way the heat does. She feels the shape of her mother in the words—the wet cloths, the flour-dust, the terror in loving eyes—and for a moment she wants nothing in the world but to be small, to be clay, to be safe. She means it. She means it with her whole body. She wants to forget the child and never have to carry her into the pyre. She wants to die with a clean weight, a list of crimes she can close.

The prayer fails.

It fails the way a stone falls in a pool with no water. No sound. No ripple. No answer. The dress is still burning behind her eyes. The child is still on the balcony. The heartbeat is still unsteady, still hers, still the only thing the fire ever gave her that she did not have to feed. She understands, in the silence after the prayer, that she did not pray to the Chastened Flame at all. You cannot pray for forgetfulness to a god of borders and locked things. Forgetting is what the city does. Forgetting is what Vane will do tomorrow, when her body is smoke and he stands at his window with a clean conscience. The Chastened Flame is the god of that forgetting. It would take the child from her gladly. It would launder her guilt into ashes and call the ashes justice.

But it did not answer. Perhaps it cannot. Perhaps even a god of locked things cannot unlock a memory. Or perhaps the only true thing she has ever said in prayer was the asking itself, and the asking is a kind of holding. To ask to forget is already to remember. The prayer cancels itself. The dress burns on.

The fever settles a little. She lies on the wet stone with her hands flat, and the crescents in her palms are cool now, empty of heat. She does not pray again. She does not try to justify again. She does not build the item column and she does not feed it to the Arsonist. She carries the child the only way a person can carry an unreturnable thing: by not putting her down. She will be tied to the pillar and the wood will stack around her, and the child will be there—on the balcony, both hands on the brick, the dress glowing, the mouth open, the sound not yet coming. Vex keeps the memory close. It is the only honest thing she has left. In a quiet hollow where neither the Arsonist nor the Penitent can reach, she hopes it will be the last thing she sees when the fire finally takes her. Not the fire. The child. The child it should never have eaten.

She says it aloud, into the dark, the way she said *Thistle, I am sorry*. She says: "I will remember you. I will remember you when I burn."

The cell absorbs it. The drip keeps time. Behind the wall, very faint, patient as a question: one. Then two. Then a pause. Then one.

She does not answer. But she does not look away from the balcony, either.

chapters.name: The Block That Moves
chapters.content:
The fever broke in the night. Vex woke to a cell with edges—the damp wall, the drip, the fifty-three tally marks lined up in the dark like the faces of old acquaintances—and lay still for a long time, feeling her mind come back to her the way a hand returns to a body it has left. For days she had been smoke. Now she was a thing with weight again, with bones, with a chain, with a name the city had taken from her and that she had taken back in the dark, saying it aloud to the drip until it fitted her mouth again.

*Vex.*

She had starved. She had burned. She had prayed to a god that did not answer, and learned in the failure what the prayer had really been: a wish to forget. The Chastened Flame was the god of forgetting. She had promised instead to remember, and the promise stood. She touched it the way she touched the crescents on her palms—carefully, as though it might be hot.

Above her, through the grate, the sounds of the square had changed. Hammering, men calling to one another with festival cheer. They were building the pyre at the center of the Sanctum square, the place of her death, and she could hear them the way a condemned woman hears a neighbor building a wall: close, daily, without malice. The pyre had been in her arithmetic for weeks. There would be fire. She would stand on it. The child would be the last thing she saw, and she had promised to remember her when the burning came.

So when the sound came, she did not know it at first. The cell had taught her to name its sounds the way she had named its stones: the drip, the rat, the Sanctum bell, the grate's whine, Wyman's boot on the stair, the weather of the crowd above. This sound owned nothing. Too heavy for the rat, too deliberate for the old stone, which had settled long ago into every shape it meant to keep. Stone on stone, somewhere in the wall behind her, and it was moving.

It came again—a shift, a scrape, the sound of something heavy finding the place it had been trying to find—and then a silence, and then nothing.

Vex sat up. Her body protested in a language of empty distances; she had not eaten in days, and the fever had receded, leaving her mind's new edges standing up in her like ribs. She crawled to the damp wall on her hands and knees, the chain dragging behind her like a tail.

She found it by touch. She had traced the wall a hundred and forty courses, or a hundred and thirty-nine if you did not count the half-hidden one, and her fingers knew every stone the way a blind woman knows a face. But this stone was wrong. It was the half-hidden one—the liar, the stone she had never been able to decide about—and its edges were not the true edges of the others. Cut. Filed. The mortar around them scraped away in fine, patient grooves, and in the grooves was dust that was not the cell's dust.

Someone had been working at the stone from the other side.

The thought arrived coldly, without excitement, the way a verdict arrives. The work was old, done over many nights, a handful of dust at a time, scraped into cloth and carried away, the stone pressed back into its socket so that no one passing through would see. While she tore her nails bloody on the weeping stone. While the trial read its sentence. While they built the pyre above. Someone had been digging a door to her cell.

It did not make sense. The oubliette was supposed to be a vessel, complete, a tear in the city's keel that no one entered and no one left. A tunnel meant a digger, and a digger meant a reason, and for the first time since the fire the reason was not hers. It belonged to a stranger. It had been working toward her in the dark, and it had not stopped when she stopped praying. The thought tipped something in her chest—a thing that had been balanced for weeks.

She put her raw fingers into the gap and pulled.

The stone did not move. It was seated in its socket the way a tooth is seated in a jaw. She pulled until her arms shook and the sweat broke out on her forehead and the chain cut into her ankle, rested, pulled again. On the third pull, with a sound like the cell itself sighing, the block came free.

It settled into her lap, heavy and cold. She held it, breathing, looking at the dark it had left.

The wall was deeper than the stone. Behind the block was not more wall. There was a hollow. A darkness that was not the darkness of the cell; no drip in it, no tally marks, no slant of light. Absolute, silent, and from it came air that was not the cell's air. Cold, earthen, older, smelling faintly of rot and of something her body knew before her mind did—the smell of a place where people moved.

A tunnel. She knew it in her knees and elbows before she knew it in her head. Someone had dug a tunnel to her cell.

She did not crawl in. That came to her later, in the long quiet of the night, as the first true choice she had made since the fire. She did not reason. She did not ask the two arguing voices for permission. She knelt at the opening with the block in her hands and waited, listening.

Wyman came before the light shaft had moved its width. She knew his step before he reached the bottom of the stair—drag of the left boot, pause, bolt drawn a moment early—and felt something in her chest lock. She pushed herself against the opening, spine to the damp stone, and tried to make herself wide. The block was in her hands; she had nowhere to put it. She looked at him with the flat stare of a prisoner who expects nothing, and he took in the bread and the water where they sat, untouched.

"You look like a ghost," he said. "They'll want a body, come the day. Eat something."

He left the bread and climbed back toward the light. She listened to the bolt shoot home, and only when the silence returned did she slide aside from the opening, the sweat cooling on her back, and look into the dark she had hidden with her body.

She did not know why she had hidden it. She had not decided what the tunnel was. But her body had decided before her mind could catch up, and the decision was simple: not yet. Not until she knew what it was.

The light shaft moved across the stones. The drip kept time. She knelt at the opening until her knees went numb, listening to a silence within the silence—the held breath of the tunnel, waiting to see if she would speak.

The Arsonist spoke first. Of course. *A door. Who digs a door to a condemned cell except someone who wants you out of it? Take it. Take the dark, take the stink of earth, take the chance. Live. You owe the child your witness, and you cannot witness from ash.*

The Penitent answered without raising its voice, the way it always did. *And what will you be when you crawl out? The killer who ran. The fire that walked free while the child's dress is ash in a city that has already named you. The pyre is your truth. A door is only a longer way to the same fire.*

Both of them were right. Both of them always were. That was the trap of living with two selves: the truth was never on one side, and the silence in the middle was a place she had only begun to know—a quiet hollow where neither of them could reach, where the child in the white dress watched from a balcony that would not burn, where Thistle laughed and the sea moved without asking the Order's permission.

She looked into the tunnel's dark and found she could not answer either of them. Not for lack of words—the words were already in her throat—but because she no longer knew which self she would be speaking as.

The sound came out of the dark like the first drop of water after a long silence. Not the drip. A rhythm—one, then two, then a pause, then one. The pattern that had pressed itself through the wall for days like a question she had refused to answer. It was closer now, the stone gone, nothing between her and the hand that made it. Patient. Asking.

It stopped.

A breath—a throat cleared with deliberate softness—and then a voice. Low. Female. Careful. The voice of someone who had learned to speak where sound carries and to make every syllable count for what it buys. It came through the opening as a vibration as much as a sound, laid directly into the earth:

"Vex."

She went still. The name. Not the vessel of the Unmaking, not the witch, not the monster the city called her—her name, spoken through a hole in the wall of her cell, in a voice she had never heard.

"Vex. Are you alive?"

The words hung in the damp air. Vex opened her mouth. The word *yes* rose into her throat and stopped there, caught between the two selves like a stone too large for a doorway. The Arsonist wanted it out—*live, say the word, take the hand*—and the Penitent wanted it swallowed—*you have no right to that word; the dead do not answer for themselves, and you are only their witness*—and between them the word would not come. She sat with the block in her hands. The silence stretched, and she felt the stranger's attention waiting on the other side of the dark. Patient. Careful. Not leaving.

"Strike the stone once," the voice said. "You don't have to speak. Just strike it."

The block was in her hands. She could have lifted it and let it fall against the threshold once, a sound no louder than the drip, and the stranger would have known. The child would still be remembered at the burning. Thistle's sea would still be waiting on the far side of the world.

She did not lift the block.

She sat in the dark of her cell, in the place that had learned her breathing, and felt the word *yes* turn to ash on her tongue, and did not answer.

The silence on the other side changed. It was not anger—too steady for that—and it was not grief. It was the silence of someone adding a fact to a ledger, adjusting an arithmetic, marking something done. Then the voice came once more, quieter, no less careful:

"I'll come back."

There was the sound of a body moving away in the dark. The faint scrape of cloth on stone, a breath, a small slide of earth—and then nothing, the tunnel's silence closing over the sound the way water closes over a stone.

Vex knelt at the opening for a long time, listening. The drip. The hammering above, where they were building the place of her death. The tunnel had nothing more to give.

When her legs gave out, she lay with her cheek against the stone beside the opening, fingers on its cut edge, reading the work the way she had read the tally marks of the prisoner before her. The edge was scored with a thousand small bites—not a tool, or not only a tool; something patient and perishable had worn it away, nail and stone and will.

In one of the grooves a strand of hair was caught. Dark, fine, long enough to have been pulled, not cut.

She drew it out and held it to the shaft of light. It gleamed like a wire. It was the first proof she had touched, in all the weeks of this cell, that a living body had come near her of its own will, choosing to work through the dark toward her.

She would not have been able to say why, but she tucked the strand under the cuff of her sleeve, where the chain had rubbed her wrist raw, and did not take it out again.

She should have put the block back. It was the tooth she had knocked out of the wall, and the dark it let in was the dark of the world between things, the city's unconfessed cellar, the place beneath the place. She should have seated it in its socket, pressed the dust home, and let the cell be what it had always been—the only shape the city would let her fill.

She did not put the block back.

She held it, and the knowledge of the voice—low, female, careful, speaking her name—settled into her like a second fever, into the hollow where neither the Arsonist nor the Penitent could reach. Someone knew she existed. Someone had dug toward her, through weeks of patient scraping, through the earth under the city, to a cell where the condemned were supposed to rot without witness. Someone had dug a door to the monster's cage and called her, not by her crime, not by her sentence, but by her name.

She thought of the city above—those who whispered thanks by night and shouted *burn her* by day. One of those, or one of their kind, had climbed down into the city's throat and dug toward the woman they wanted to burn. What did they want from her? The fire in her palms. It always came back to the fire. Everyone who reached toward Vex reached for what her hands could do—the Bishop to condemn it, the crowd to gape at it, the stranger to… she did not know. That was the whole of it. She did not know.

She touched the crescents on her palms. The heat there stirred faintly, like a thing waking from a long sleep, and she let it stir. She would not feed it. But she did not push it down, either. It was the only honest thing left in her body, and now there was a door in the wall, and she did not know whether the hand reaching through the dark had reached to pull her out or to strike the match that would finish her.

Salvation, or a new kind of fire.

She could not tell. She had not been able to tell the difference for a long time—perhaps not since the night at the Founders' gates, palms smoking, believing the flame was all of these at once, door and fire and justice and the face of the beast, and that she could hold it without being changed. She had been changed. That was the one thing the fire had done truly.

The bread sat where Wyman had laid it. She reached for it, broke off a corner, ate. The crust was hard and crumbled in her mouth like mortar, and it went down like a decision.

She would not trust the voice. She would not hope—hope was a door she had not decided to walk through. But she would be alive when it came back, alive in the only way she still knew: with the dead carried inside her, the white dress burning behind her eyes, the sea in her chest like a word she had not yet found the mouth for.

The block was heavy in her hands. She did not put it back. She knelt at the meeting place of two silences—the cell's, which had learned her breathing, and the tunnel's, which had not yet learned anything—and she was not the condemned woman the city had named, not the vessel of the Unmaking, not even the self who had promised to die. She was something in between, a question at the threshold of her own story, and she did not know if the hand reaching for her through the dark was a hand that would pull her out or a hand that would light the fire.

chapters.name: The Chastened Flame
chapters.content:
The fog inside her had a texture. It was not the wet breath of the cisterns, the moss-and-cold-stone smell of the lower districts. This was a fog between one thought and the next, and Vex had learned to live in it the way a person learns to live with a limp.

She measured the days by the light shaft's crawl, by Wyman's tread, by the hammering in the Sanctum square. The pyre was taking shape. She could hear the workmen singing a festival song, something about the harvest and the mercy of the Chastened Flame. Men who built pyres did not build them in silence.

She thought about her mother.

The thought arrived without warning, the way the deep ones did, rising through the fog like a stone through water. Her mother's hands, flour-dusted, knuckle-deep in dough, moving with the economy of a woman who had made the same bread ten thousand times. Vex had watched those hands the way other children watched birds, with a stillness that was pure attention.

The bakery on Ash Lane came back in smells: yeast breathing in the dark, burned sugar where a batch of festival loaves had been left too long, the wood of the counter polished by generations of palms. She had been small, barefoot on the brick floor, standing close to the great oven while her mother shaped loaves and sang the Order's hymns under her breath. The hymns were all about fire. Fire as the breath of the god, fire locked in the censer, the candle, the altar lamp, burning where it was given leave to burn.

"Don't stand so close," her mother said.

"I'm not close."

She was close enough to feel the oven's breath on her face, a warm hand pressing her cheek. She liked it. The heat wrapped around her without burning, bending the way her mother's arms bent around her in the winter cold. She had not felt cold since she could remember. The cold was a thing other people wore—shawls and red hands and stamped feet—a story they told her, and she nodded because it was easier than explaining.

She was four, or five. Pell, the apprentice with the wandering mind, had dropped a sack of flour. The sack burst across the brick floor, a white cloud blooming, and Vex stood in the middle of it, dragging a wooden spoon through the drifts, making roads and rivers in the white.

Pell told her to get out of the way. She looked up at him with the word *no* in her throat, and she was angry.

The anger was a warm thing. It woke in her chest, a kitten uncurling, and stretched its claws. The flour at her feet began to smoke.

She did not see it at first. She was looking at Pell, and the heat pooled in her hands, the familiar warmth she had always thought everyone felt when they were angry. But the warmth had a direction now. It had an intention, and the intention was the flour, the white cloud between her and the boy.

The flour smoldered. A curl of white smoke rose. Pell stopped talking.

Time went strange. Her mother moved past her, fast for a woman who kneaded all day, snatched a wet cloth from the table, stamped the smoldering drift into silence. The smoke curled into the rafters and died.

Then her mother's hands on her shoulders, turning her. The expression on her face was not anger; her mother's anger was a quiet tightening of the mouth. This was fear. Vex had seen fear in the ration lines, in the faces of mothers whose children cried with thirst. She had never seen her mother wear it.

"Your hands. Show me your hands."

Vex held them out. Small hands, flour-dusted, unburned. They were always unburned. The crescents lay in her palms, pale and smooth, like marks left by a coin pressed into clay. Her mother stared at them, her thumb moving over the left crescent as if she could rub it away.

She led Vex to the back room, the one with the cot and the basin. She soaked a rag in cold water, knelt, and took Vex's hands in her own.

"This will be wet and cold."

"I'm not cold."

"I know." Her mother wrapped the wet cloth around her right hand, folding it carefully. The cold bit into her skin. Vex did not struggle. She understood that she was being wrapped in a law.

"Water and fire do not like each other," her mother said, reaching for the second cloth. "The Order says we are to keep fire where it belongs. In the candle. In the censer. In the oven. Fire that is not where it belongs is not a servant. It is a stray. It is a sin."

"I didn't mean to."

Her mother finished wrapping the second hand and took Vex's face in her damp hands. The fear in her eyes was a private thing, older than Vex, carried into the marriage and up the stairs of the bakery. It was the fear of a woman who had known something about fire and hoped her child would not know it too.

"Listen to me. This does not leave this room. I will tell Pell it was the flour catching a spark from the oven. I will tell him whatever I need to tell him. There are people in this city who would take a child who makes fire in her hands and call her a vessel of the Unmaking. They would put her in a cage and burn her, and they would call it the mercy of the Chastened Flame. And I would die before I let anyone take you."

"Yes, Mama."

"Then promise me. Promise me you will be careful. Promise me you will be small. Promise me you will not let them see."

"I promise, Mama."

The water was cold on the crescents, and the promise sat inside her like a stone in a loaf. She kept it for years. When the heat woke in her hands, which it did more and more as she grew, she pressed her palms flat to the brick floor, or buried them in the ash pit behind the oven, or held them under the pump in the yard until her fingers went white.

The Order of the Chastened Flame was Meridian's religion of pure order, learned at her mother's knee and at the knees of the priests who came to bless the ovens at the festival of the kindling. The doctrine was simple, and its simplicity made it strong. Fire was a servant, but a servant required a master. Unmastered fire was not fire; it was heresy, the Unmaking, the devouring dark before the god's work. Every hand that made its own flame was a hand reaching back into the chaos, un-building the world. The first fire-killer had been a woman who ate the tongue of the god and took the fire into her mortal flesh. She had walked through the land burning crops and herds and homes, and when the god caught her he had caged her, put the fire into candles and censers where it could serve, and marked her line for all time. A vessel of the Unmaking was a body that carried that fire in its blood, waiting to wake. The priests watched for children who burned where they should not burn, at boneless curtsies and hideth. Vex sat in the Sanctum between her mother and her sister and felt the crescents itch.

At night, her mother prayed over her cot. The words were a physical thing, the way she remembered the pull of dough.

*Flame of Order, chasten her hands. Let her burn only what she is given. Let her be a candle, not a fire. Make her clay, not coal. Make her small. Make her safe.*

Vex lay under the prayers, trying to become the candle her mother asked for. She imagined herself a small contained flame in a glass, burning where she was placed, never escaping. But the image would not hold. The heat in her palms was not a candle's heat. It was a hunger's heat, a thing that wanted to run.

"Or at the Order family"—"The Order says—" she began once at the table.

Her mother's hand came down flat on the wood, a crack of silence.

"The Order says," her mother said, in the quietest voice Vex had ever heard, "that fire is a servant. I have served the Order all my life. I have kneaded the bread and kept the ovens and said the prayers. And I am telling you, child, you belong to me first. The Order has never kneaded a loaf in its life. It does not know the closeness of a mother's hands to her child's. It does not get to take you."

There was something in the words Vex did not yet have a name for. It was the sound of a cage being bent, not opened, but bent.

"The Order is the order of the city," her mother went on. "The Founders keep the water, the Order keeps the fire, the people keep their place, and the world continues to turn. That is the bargain I have made for you. You will keep your hands hidden. You will pray. You will be small. And the world will not take you from me."

"Yes, Mama."

"You will not burn. Do you understand? You will not want to burn anything. You will want what I want for you: a quiet life, a bakery of your own. You will want those things until the wanting is true."

"Yes, Mama."

Her mother looked at her for a long moment, and Vex looked back, and she wanted to say, *But I do want to burn things. I want to burn the Founders' gates. I want to burn the locked cisterns. I want to burn the healer's door that closes at dusk. I want to burn the whole world flat and clean, and grow something better in the ashes.*

She said nothing. She hid her hands in her apron and went to fetch the flour. The wanting sat inside her like the oven's breath, warm and patient, and she fed it with her silence, one piece at a time.

It did not go away. It grew with her. She grew taller, and the crescents grew with her, pale and smooth, like scars that had never closed. She learned to count faster, to press her palms against the cold stone of the ash pit until the wanting sank into her cells. She learned to be ordinary, to be small. The neighbors saw a quiet girl, a baker's daughter, hands hidden in her apron. The Order's visitors saw a child who curtsied and did not stare at the censer. She spent her free hours at the back of the bakery, feeding the oven and watching the flames through the iron door. The flames did not feel like a temptation. They felt like recognition.

In the oubliette, the fog shifted. The memory folded itself away, a loaf returned to the shelf.

Vex lay in the dark with her hands on the wet stone. Behind the fog she could see the shape of the truth she had been circling for days: she had hidden the fire all her life because she was told to, because the Order called it a sin, because her mother had bound her hands in wet cloths and whispered prayers over her. She had learned that her gift was shameful, a crack in the Order's orderly world, a thing that must never see the light. She had learned to be small.

And then the fire had seen the light. She had let it out—not because it had snarled and broken her, but because she had chosen. She had spent years learning smallness as a protection, and then Marnie had died, and the healer's door was shut, and the cage had not saved anyone. In the moment she understood that, she had chosen to be a fire instead.

She pressed her palms flat against the stone. The crescents woke, not with warmth—she had not allowed them to wake since the fever—but with the memory of warmth, a phantom heat that raised no smoke. A choice was a thing you could not unsay. She could repent it, be sorry for it, beg to be forgiven and be refused, and still the choice would stand, loaves on a shelf.

She turned her head. The block was still loose, the dark of the tunnel still open behind her. Someone had dug a door to the monster's cage and called her by her name. She had not answered. She had not sealed it.

She rose. Her knees cracked. The bread she had eaten had given her back a little of her body. She went to the wall, knelt, and put her hand into the opening, feeling the fine, patient grooves, the cold air on her fingers. She did not crawl in. She had not decided that. But she did not pull back, either. She sat with her palm open in the dark, the crescents bare, and she said, to the silence, to the memory of the voice, to the unanswered question of her own life:

"I'm here."

chapters.name: The Hands That Burned
chapters.content:
The morning the pyre-builders stopped hammering, Vex heard them testing the wood. Thump, thump, thump—a fist against a barrel, searching for hollows. She had learned to sort their sounds the way she had once sorted the sounds of the bakery: the grind of the mill, the slap of dough, the oven door sighing on its hinge. Above her, men were choosing the wood that would hold her fast.

She had been eating. Wyman's bread, white and soft, the ration bread that had once been a Founder's luxury. She chewed slowly, and the taste was yeast and salt, and it opened a door in her she had not meant to open.

---

The bakery on Ash Lane smelled of yeast and woodsmoke and her mother's sweat. Vex knew it by touch, by the hurts that lived in it. Flour sacks leaned against the far wall, soft white bodies breathing dust. The oven took up half the wall and gave back heat like an animal breathing. By the time she was eight she was apprenticed to her own mother's bakery, which meant rising before the sun, hauling water from the pump, and taking the blame for whatever the other apprentice broke.

Pell was twelve, too tall for his smock, flour creased into the backs of his hands. He was not cruel the way monsters are cruel; he was cruel the way boys are cruel who have learned cruelty is a currency. He flicked dough at her neck. He called her Paddlehands, for the scars. He took credit for her loaves and gave her blame for his burned ones, and her mother said nothing, because her mother was afraid, and the fear wore many faces but the mouth was always the same: *stay small, stay quiet, let it pass.*

Vex stayed small. She stayed quiet. She let it pass, and she hated it, and beneath the hatred—folded like dough, kneaded smooth—was the wanting. A wanting with a shape.

---

The day it happened, Pell had been chosen to deliver the Founder's order, a standing commission of white loaves for the festivals. The honor went to his head. He swaggered through the bakery with his thumbs in his apron, telling the flour-miller's boy how it would be when he was a master baker, with his own ovens and his own apprentices to haul.

"And her," Pell said, jerking his chin at Vex. "Hands like paddles, strong for a girl." The flour-miller's boy laughed, because laughter was cheaper than a bruise.

Vex kept her head down, kneading the festival dough. *Stay small. Stay quiet. Let it pass.*

"Paddlehands," Pell said, coming closer. "You ever wonder why your ma wraps your hands in wet rags? She think they'll drift off without the water to hold 'em down?"

It was the wet rags that did it. Everyone in the bakery had seen the rags; no one had ever named them. He should not have known what they were for.

Vex looked up. Flour hung in the air—there was always flour in the air—and she wanted him to stop. Not to hurt him. Just to stop. The wanting opened in her chest like a hand unfolding.

The flour caught the way lightning happens: not a growth, but a jump. A line of flame ran up through the flour-fog, out from her hands, a rope of fire that found the nearest sack and bit. Pell screamed and fell backward, and the flour-miller's boy ran, and Vex stood with her hands open, the crescents gleaming, watching the fire eat her mother's flour.

For one second—the whole second of her life she would try and fail to dig out of herself—it felt good. The fire was her wanting, out where she could see it. It was loud. It was honest. It said everything she had never been allowed to say.

Then her mother was there. A shape inside the smoke, beating at the sacks with wet sackcloth, her voice a blade: *water, get the water.* Vex ran for the pump. The water came up cold and brown, and her mother threw it on the fire, and the fire hissed and spat and threw up steam, and her mother beat it, beat it, beat it, until the last flame guttered out in black paste.

The bakery stood. Barely. Pell crouched in a corner, his eyebrows gone, crying without sound. The flour-miller's boy was gone entirely. Vex stood in the smoking silence, the bucket in her hands, and she knew her mother had seen.

Her mother did not speak in front of Pell. She hauled him up, felt his face with careful hands, told him he was lucky the fire could have taken his eyes. Then she told them all what had happened: the lantern by the flour. The draft from the door. The flour dust had done what flour dust does. Pell, shaking, nodded. Pell, who would have run to the Order with a girl who made fire from her hands, accepted the lantern, because the alternative was a truth too terrible to hold. The story was good. The story was even true, in the way all lies are true—with one fact cut out of the middle.

---

Her mother did not speak until the bakery was clean. They scrubbed the black from the walls and carried the ruined sacks to the ash pits, where the ground was still warm from the day's baking. All through it, her mother's hands moved, her mother's mouth was shut, and Vex moved to match her, drowning in the silence. She had broken the promise. The wanting had stood up in her chest and shown itself.

The moment came at dusk, in the yard behind the bakery. They had thrown the last of the ruined flour onto the pile. Her mother stood looking at it, her shadow long across the yard.

"Look at me."

Vex looked. Her mother's face was not angry. It was worse. It was the face of a woman reading a sentence she had known was coming for years.

"You used it," her mother said. "Not dropped it. Not lost it. *Used* it." She took Vex's hands, turned them over, stared at the crescents. "Tell me truly. Do you know how you did it?"

Vex tried to explain the wanting. The shape of it. How it had opened in her chest like a hand, and the fire had outrun her intention before she had known she intended. How it had felt good.

Her mother listened, her hands wrapped around Vex's, shaking—not with fear. Something finer, harder. When Vex finished, her mother said, "It was the lantern. Do you understand? It was the lantern. The draft and the dust. That is what happened. That is the whole of it. If anyone asks—anyone at all, the Order, the Bishop, a man with a badge—that is the truth you will swallow and hold, and you will never let it out with your face or your hands or your eyes. Do you understand?"

"Yes, Ma."
