Her mother pulled her into her arms, fierce, smelling of smoke. "You belong to me. I will die before I let anyone take you. But you have to help me keep you, Vex. You have to be small."

Vex made the promise. *I will be careful. I will be small. I will not let them see.* She meant it the way a drowning girl means to hold her breath. That night, when her mother prayed over her cot—*Flame of Order, chasten her hands. Let her burn only what she is given. Let her be a candle, not a fire*—Vex lay still and tried to be a candle. Candles did not want.

And the wanting sat in her chest, folded, kneaded smooth, already rising. It had tasted air. It knew what it was now: not a candle's heat, but a hunger's. It could wait.

---

She practiced.

This was the secret after the secret. Her mother believed the lesson had taken. Part of Vex had swallowed it whole—but another part had discovered its body.

Behind the ash pits, a fallen wall made a hollow out of sight of the kitchen windows. Vex went there in the hour before curfew, when her mother was shaping the next day's dough and the risk of being missed was small.

At first she was afraid. She held a twig in her hands and wanted it to light. Nothing. She tried harder. Still nothing. Frustration gathered in her chest, and a spark jumped from her palm and died on the twig, leaving a bead of black.

The discovery came slowly, by trial and error and singed fingers. The fire answered to wanting, not to effort. When she strained, her wanting closed like a fist, and the fire could not pass. When she let it open—when she thought of the thing she wanted to consume and let the wanting uncurl toward it—the heat ran down her arm and out through her palm. Twig. Curl of paper. Knot of straw. Once, a beetle, by accident. She buried its shell under a stone and never burned anything living again.

She could hold flame in her bare palm; the heat bent around her skin the way water bends around a stone. It was not mere heat. It was will. She could set things alight with a thought—not a word, not a gesture, but the same invisible muscle that moved her hands, aimed, released. She learned that anger made it fast and hungry, and that hunger was hard to call back. She learned that fear made it gutter. She learned that love made it behave.

The word came to her from the Order's own sermons: purification. The Order said fire purified, that the Chastened Flame burned out the rot. Vex had thought they meant a threat. But sitting in the hollow, watching a knot of rye-straw burn to perfect white ash, she began to think they had meant a description. Fire took what was and made it into something else. It consumed the rot and left clean ash, ready to feed better things.

The wanting took on a shape she could believe. It was not destruction. It was judgment.

She dreamed of burning things. Never people—gates, locks, doors. She walked through the Founders' Quarter in her dreams, though she had never been there; in the dream she knew every gate. The locked cisterns fell open. The healer's door that closed at dusk burned in its frame. The world went flat and clean, and out of the ashes she grew something better: a warm, flour-dusted room that smelled of yeast, and the pumps ran freely, and everyone drank.

She never whispered the dream aloud. The promise held. She was careful. She was small. She did not let them see. And the dream grew in the dark of her like a loaf rising.

---

Then Marnie was born.

It was a hard birth. Vex was sent out of the room into the oven room, to keep the fires fed and stay out of the way. She fed the ovens. She shaped tomorrow's dough. She worked the familiar motions and did not allow herself to think about the screams.

It was dusk when the house went quiet. The quiet was worse than the screams.

Vex stood in the doorway, flour to her elbows, and the midwife came out and said, "A girl. You can come see, if you want."

She went. The room smelled of blood and sweat and something new. Her mother lay propped on the bed, pale and radiant, the particular fierceness of a woman who had survived her body's worst work. In the crook of her arm, wrapped in clean cloth, was a small red thing with its eyes open.

"Vex," her mother said, hoarse. "Come and meet your sister."

Vex came. The crescents in her palms prickled—not fire, but something with no name yet. She was afraid to touch the small red thing. What if the wanting woke? What if she marked the child the way she was marked?

Her mother took her wrist, gently, and guided her hand. "It's all right. She's not afraid."

Vex touched the baby's head. The hair was fine and soft as flour-dust. Marnie—her mother had saved the name for years—turned toward her sister's hand. Her eyes, impossibly awake, found Vex's face.

There was no fear in them. Vex had seen fear in a thousand eyes. Marnie looked at her, and there was no fear. There was wonder. Recognition—as if the newborn had known her, had been expecting her, had chosen her sister as the one thing in the whole strange world worth meeting. Frank. Fearless. Adoring.

Vex laughed. It was the first true laugh since the day her hands had shown themselves, and the sound surprised her. She bent her head close and let the baby's fingers close around one of her own, a small fierce grip, the whole body intent on holding her.

"Hello, Marnie," she whispered. "I'm Vex. I'm your sister. I'm going to keep you safe."

The crescents itched. The wanting stirred, folded, patient as a coal under ash. Marnie did not know anything—what her sister could do, what her sister had dreamed, the fire sleeping in the same hands that held her head. Marnie looked at Vex, and the adoration was clean.

Vex made the vow in the silence of her chest. She would be small. She would be careful. She would bury the wanting so deep no one would ever find it, so this small, fearless thing could live in a world where fire stayed where it belonged: in candles, in censers, in ovens.

She would be small, for Marnie.

The dream rose behind her eyes—the locked cisterns falling open, the healer's door burning in its frame, the world flat and clean. She put it away like a mother putting a child to bed. She did not need it anymore. She had this.

Marnie yawned. Vex laughed again, and Marnie's eyes—already going drowsy, already knowing she was safe—closed.

---

The cell was cold.

Vex came back to herself with the bread half-eaten in her hand and her cheek wet. The hammering had stopped. Through the grate, the evening bell of the Sanctum rang, and somewhere in the city a child was laughing, and the sound was the same as it had ever been.

She looked at her own hands. The crescents were pale, quiet. The wanting was a coal under ash.

Marnie had held these hands. Marnie had looked into her face and seen nothing to fear. And years later, when the fire went out of her hands into the Founders' Quarter, Marnie was already dead—not of the fire, but of the thirst and the fever that came with locked cisterns, with the healer's door that closed at dusk. The fire had been for her. It had not brought her back.

"Small," Vex whispered to the stone. "Careful. Safe."

The words no longer fit her. She had grown past them the way a fire grows past the hearth it was meant to warm.

Above her, the pyre waited. Below her, the tunnel waited. And in her chest, the coal under the ash was patient as ever. Marnie had been the only one who ever knew her and was never afraid, and the only comfort left was that: the adoration had been clean, and she had repaid it with fire and failure, and she would carry both to the pillar and let them burn.

She pressed her palms flat against the cold stone.

"Hello, Marnie," she whispered into the dark. "I'm still your sister. I'm still sorry."

The stone did not answer. But somewhere above, the child's laughter ran on, bright and careless, and Vex closed her eyes, and she held the memory of the newborn's grip around her finger like a candle flame cupped against the wind.

chapters.name: The Water Ledgers
chapters.content:
The drip was the first thing she heard when she woke, and the last thing she heard before sleep took her. She counted it the way the prisoner before her had counted days. One. Two. Three. A pause that held its breath, then a small rush, fast as a heart remembering fear. The cell wept water from the stone, and the water ran down to a drain she had never found, and it tasted of old iron and a coin, and she could not drink it. She had spent her whole life in a city that measured water with a tight fist. Now she lay in a cell that wept it into the dark, and the sound of it was the worst sound she knew.

Water. Her memory had been circling it for days, the way the tongue circles a broken tooth. Water in a bucket. Water behind iron. Water that ran day and night for the sound of it. Water that had once been somebody's wedding ring.

The summer she was thirteen.

The sky sat on the city like a lid, the color of unwashed linen, and the heat pressed down the chimney and lay across the bakery like a patient hand. Ash Lane wore its dust like a second skin—on the shutters, in the bread baskets, in the seams of her mother's cracked palms. The common well behind the tailor's shop went from sweet to bitter to brackish inside a month. You could smell the change before you saw it: old rope and old pennies and something green dying under the heat. The well had been a meeting place, then a ration line, then a sentence.

The Founders' water carts ran on schedule.

That was the fact that sharpened her. The cruelty was not chaos; it was method. It moved on wheels, an iron-bound cart of varnished oak, the Founders' seal burned into the side—a hand holding a cup above a cistern, and beneath it, so small she had to stand close to read it, *WE GUARD WHAT WE HOLD*. The cart passed down Ash Lane every fourth day at dusk, drawn by a bay horse better fed than any child on the lane. The driver was a Founders' man in gray, and his whip was not for the horse but for the children. The children ran beside the cart anyway, barefoot, holding out their buckets—dented, borrowed, already a child's weight in their arms—shouting *water, water* as if the cart were a festival float and they were begging sweetmeats. The driver never turned. The cart went on. The dust rose. The water went to the Founders' Quarter, to the fountain that ran day and night for the sound of it. No one on the lane had ever heard the fountain. They had only been told to be grateful it made their Founders happy.

Vex watched this happen nine times before she learned to leave her bucket at home.

The public board stood at the corner of the rag market under a tin awning rusted the color of blood. Ration schedules. The new water law: *one bucket per family of five, per day, at the north cistern, between the second and third bells, proof of residence required*. Beneath the law, a page from the Founders' own water ledger, nailed up as proof the ration was just—columns of figures with each district's name above them, and the lower districts' column crossed out in iron-red ink: *closed until rains*. The rains had not come.

Beside the notices, pinned with the same iron nails, someone had posted the Founders' menu for the Feast of the Chaste Flame. *A cream served in cups of cistern ice.*

The words hung in her like a fishhook.

The women in the rag market read the menu aloud the way they read funeral announcements—quietly, without surprise. "Cistern ice," said the seamstress who sewed the Founders' gowns. "They have so much water they can freeze it and eat it off a spoon." She did not sound angry. The heat had burned the anger out of some women and banked it deep in others, and the seamstress was one of the others; Vex could see it in the line of her shoulders, a coal under gray ash.

Then the priest passed through the market, a sanctified censer swinging, the licensed fire swaying in its iron cage. "Suffering is the god's test," he said in a carrying voice. "The Founders hold the water because the god has charged them with its keeping. Your thirst is a trial, and your endurance is the god's proof of love. Do not envy the keepers. Pray for the strength to pass the test."

Vex stood at the edge of the shade with the delivery basket in her arms and felt the words turn in her chest. *The test is written by the testers. They grade the papers they set themselves. They pass themselves.* It was worse than that. A trial was a fire you were given to walk through. This was a fire they built, and kept building, and called providence.

The next day, the seamstress came to the common well with her wedding ring in her palm.

She had been first in line when the well was sweet; Vex remembered old mornings, the crank singing, the needle-pricked fingers. Now she stood at the lip of the brackish dark with two small children behind her, and the water-seller—a man with a license and a barrel and the face of a man doing a job he hated—said the price had gone up. The well was low. His barrel was all he had to sell. Coin, or nothing.

The seamstress held out her ring. A thin gold thing, worn smooth by twenty years of work. "I haven't any coin."

"It's not coin."

"It's gold."

The water-seller took it. He weighed it in his hand the way he weighed everything, without malice, then bit it the way men bit coins. He filled the bucket. He did not fill it to the brim—the measure was a measure, and he had his license to think of, and a man could only push against the order of things so far before the order caught up with him. The water was the color of weak tea, with a thin film across it. The seamstress took the bucket with both hands and lifted it like a holy thing. Dry eyes. A mouth shaped into a smile. "It's only a ring. I can't drink a ring."

The children looked at the water. Everyone at the well looked at the water—the brackish, short-measured, bought-with-a-marriage water. The seamstress had sewn the gowns the Founders wore to the feast where the cream was served in ice. The hands that wore that ring had carried those gowns. Now it was trade. A half-measure of bad water. A coin with a marriage worn into it.

The want stirred in the hollow of Vex's chest. Not the crackling want she practiced behind the ash pits, the one that answered to her will and the set of her hands. This was the other kind, the one with eyes. It came up slow, like dough, and it did not want to make anything. It wanted to correct.

Her mother saw it on her face before she was through the door.

"Don't," her mother said.

"I haven't said anything."

"You don't have to. It's on you like a flush. Sit down." She poured from the small pitcher they kept by the window—clean water, rationed even inside the bakery, saved for the dough and the children. The pitcher held less than it had last week. "Sit. Drink. Let it go."

"Did you see the menu?" Vex heard herself ask. "They drink cream out of cups of ice. While the tailor's wife sold her ring for a bucket of bad water. And the Order says—"

"The Order says suffering is a test." Her mother's hands never stopped kneading; the dough met the board with a sound like a pulse. "I know what the Order says. I have said it myself a thousand times standing in this kitchen, because it was what I could afford to say. It is what I can afford to say now. But you can't say it, Vex. Not with your face doing what it's doing. Not in this house, where I have kept you hidden."

"How is a locked cistern a test?" Vex said. The words came out smaller than she meant them to, quieter, the kind of quiet that carries. "If the god wanted to test us, he would give us a chance to pass. The Founders have the water and the key. They write the test and hold the answer, and when we fail, they call it good. That isn't a trial. That's a ledger."

Her mother's hands stopped. The dough held the shape of hands.

"I don't care what you burned," she said softly. "I care that you burned." She came around the bench, wiped her hands on her apron, and took Vex's hands in hers. The crescents lay against her palms, pale, quiet. "The Founders keep the water. The Order keeps the fire. The people keep their place, and the world continues to turn. That is the bargain. I made it the day your hands showed themselves, and I have kept my end by keeping you small. You promised me you would be small. You promised me careful. You promised me you would not let them see."

Vex's silence went on too long.

"Then you have broken it already," her mother said. "In your hands, if not in the world. If I could burn it all, I would—the cart and the well and the key and the great Founders' feast, and I would not weep for one silken ribbon. But I cannot burn it. I can only keep you. And if you burn it, they will not ask whose hunger lit the match. They will see the fire, and they will call you the Unmaking, and they will take you from me. I will die before I let them take you—but I am asking you, on the promise you made me, not to make me watch you carry the fire to them yourself."

Marnie came in from the yard, small and solemn, a dust-smear across her cheek. She held out her tin cup with the blue rim, the one she carried to bed like a blessing. "Mama. There's no more."

Her mother filled the cup from the pitcher without measuring—half a cup. Marnie drank it slowly, obediently, eyes wide over the rim, the way the seamstress had carried her bucket, carefully, as if the water could be persuaded to stay. When she was done, she held the cup out again, and her mother said, "That's all, love," and Marnie nodded and did not ask again.

Vex watched her sister turn the cup in her small hands, turning the blue rim to the light, looking for another drop. The trust was still there, the fearless trust that the world would be held by someone safe. The want that had been a coal under ash broke open and showed its appetite. Not the bright crackling want she could aim and call and hold in a bare palm. This was the one kneaded into shape by the same hands that prayed over her at night. It would not be satisfied with gates.

That night, when the bakery was dark and her mother's breathing had evened into the rhythm of prayer given up for the day, Vex slipped out the back door and crossed the yard to the hollow behind the ash pits.

The moon was up, pale as the lid of the sky. The stone she had buried the beetle under still stood there, a small gray sentinel. Vex sat down in the place that knew her practice, opened her hand, and called the fire.

It came willingly. It always came willingly now. She held it in her palm, a small steady tongue of gold, and felt its hunger lean toward her like a dog's, and made it walk her knuckles one by one. Beautiful. Obedient. A creature of will and want and nothing else.

She did not call anger. Anger was fast and hungry and hard to call back. She called the other thing—the corrector, the one that had stood up inside her at the rag market, at the well, at the sight of her sister turning a tin cup to the light. She called the want, straight and pure, and said to it in the language of heat and willingness: *Not them. Not the seamstress. Not the children. Not the ring in the water-seller's fist. The gates. The cart. The key. The ledger that says a wedding ring is worth less than a bucket of bad water.*

The flame bent toward her words the way a fire bends toward a wind. It wanted the gates. It wanted the cart. It wanted to walk the Founders' Quarter and eat the menu and drink the cream until nothing was left but clean ash and clean water running over the stones.

It had found its injustice.

Vex closed her hand on it. The heat bent around her skin; she was the one thing she had burned and could not burn. She sat in the dark with her fist pressed to her chest and made a promise, the way her mother measured water: *I will aim it. I will open the gates. I will keep Marnie safe from the bucket and the ring and the menu. I will burn the ledgers—not the people.*

She did not know yet that the want, once named, had begun to outgrow the shape she poured it into. She did not know the ledgers had faces.

The memory folded away like a hand closing. In the cell, the drip went on measuring the dark, the water of the city's walls running down to a drain that would not drink it.

Vex lay with her cheek against the stone and said, quietly, to the seamstress and the ring and the tin cup: "I aimed it. I meant the gates."

The stone did not answer.

Somewhere above her, the pyre waited. The want sat in her chest, patient as a key in a lock, a coal under ash. And the drip went on—one, two, three, pause, and the small rush after, like a heart remembering fear. Measuring the dark not by time but by water. The only ledger Meridian had ever known how to keep.

chapters.name: Marnie
chapters.content:
The drip stopped. Vex lay with her spine against the stone and listened to the silence where the drip should be, and then the small rush came, the pause that held its breath, the single drop striking the floor like a coin into a cup. She let the rhythm find her, the way her mother's hands found the rhythm of dough in the dark hours before the ovens woke, and she let herself remember.

Marnie had been born during the long coughing winter, when the wells froze and the Founders' fountains ran with steam. Vex had been put in the oven room while the screaming went on—someone had to keep the loaves rising—and she had kneaded bread through her sister's first hour in the world, her palms leaving crescents in the dough that baked into the crust like a secret only the bread would know.

When the dusk quiet came, her mother's voice found her through the door, thin as candle smoke: "Come and see."

The room smelled of blood and sweat and something green, the smell of a body that had done a hard thing. Her mother lay in the bed, radiant and exhausted, and in the hollow of her arm lay a small red thing with its eyes open.

"Her name is Marnie," her mother said. "I saved it for her."

Vex did not ask why. She did not need to. Her mother had said once, in the dark of the bakery, that she had wanted to name her first child after the sea, if there had been a sea in Meridian. Marnie was the closest the lower districts had to a wave.

"Touch her wrist," her mother said. "She'll grip if you're lucky."

Vex was afraid. The crescents pricked her palms—not fire, but something colder, a warning with no language—and she was afraid the wanting would wake and mark the child the way it had marked her. She stood frozen, and her mother watched her with eyes that saw too much and said nothing.

"Vex. Touch her wrist."

She reached out, slow. The small red thing turned its head—impossibly, as if it had been waiting—and fastened its eyes on her face. Gray, the way all newborn eyes are gray, the color of the sky before rain. And the tiny fingers closed around her thumb with shocking strength, and held.

"Hello, Marnie," Vex said. Her voice came out strange, scraped clean. "I'm Vex. I'm your sister. I'm going to keep you safe."

In the silence of her chest, she made the vow her mother would never know of: she would be small. She would be careful. She would bury the wanting so deep no one would ever find it. She would be a candle, not a fire. For this.

Marnie held her thumb all through the night. The warmth of those small fingers stayed in her hand for days, like a coal that would not cool.

Marnie walked late and talked early. By the time she was three, she had opinions about everything and expressed them at length. She followed Vex through the bakery like a small determined shadow, a running commentary on the world: the flour sacks were elephants, the oven was a dragon, the rats in the alley were the Founders' tiny spies.

"Don't let the Order hear you say that," Vex said once.

Marnie looked up, eyes guileless and sharp as a pin. "Why not? The Order doesn't own the rats."

"The Order doesn't own anything," Vex said, before she could stop herself. The words hung in the flour-fogged air. She had never said anything like that aloud. Her mother's warning was a physical memory in her chest: *small, careful, do not let them see.*

Marnie was not afraid. She nodded as if Vex had confirmed something she already knew, then went back to building a city out of breadcrumbs.

"Don't tell Mama," Vex said.
"I won't."
"Promise me."

Marnie looked up, solemn for exactly two seconds, then grinned with a mouth full of borrowed raisins. "I promise I won't tell Mama you said that. But I might tell her you put too much water in the dough, because you do."

The raisin-stealing had become a ritual by then. The baklery's supply lived in a clay jar on the highest shelf. Marnie would stand beneath it with her arms stretched up, as if she could summon raisins through desire. Vex would walk past, reach the jar down without looking, tilt it toward Marnie's cupped hands, and walk on. Marnie never said thank you. She showed it in a wink, a crumb of stolen raisin left deliberately on the workbench, the performance of not-seeing both of them maintained when their mother asked where the jar's contents had gone.

Marnie's questions came at odd hours and odd places—kneading dough in the gray pre-dawn, shelling peas on the back step. Some were simple: *Why is the moon smaller some nights? Does the oven get tired?* Some were harder: *Why does the Founders' fountain run all day and no one drinks from it? Why does the healer lock her door before the bell?* Vex answered the simple ones. The hard ones she answered with silence, or with another question, or by finding Marnie something to do. But Marnie had a memory for unanswered questions. She stored them with her stolen raisins and brought them out at unexpected moments, still fresh, still demanding.

"Why does the Order say fire is bad?"

The question came in the oven room at dusk, when the flames were safely caged behind the iron door. Marnie was six, cross-legged on a sack of flour, chin in her hands.

"The Order doesn't say fire is bad," Vex said carefully. "Fire is holy when it's in its place. In candles. In censers. In the oven. Fire outside its place—"

"Is the Unmaking," Marnie finished, in the sing-song of a child reciting a lesson. "But the Bishop says the Unmaking is a dark thing. A thing that devours. But you look at the oven like it's your friend."

The words stopped Vex's hands. She turned, flour up to her elbows, and looked at her sister—small, serious, unafraid.

"I like the warmth," Vex said.

"You look at it like it's talking to you."

"It does talk. It tells me when the bread is ready. When the oven is too hot, when it's going to burn the bottoms of the loaves. You learn to listen."

Marnie considered this. "Does it ever tell you to do things? The fire?"

The question was guileless. But Vex felt the coal in her chest stir, and she crushed it down with the whole weight of her will.

"No. Fire doesn't tell you to do things. You tell it. You're always the one in charge."

"Good," Marnie said, returning to the raisin ledger she was keeping on a scrap of paper. "Because I'd hate to have to tell Mama you're friends with a dangerous thing."

"She knows. She's the one who taught me."

Marnie looked up, then. For a long moment, her small face was unreadable. Then she went back to her ledger, and the moment passed, and Vex told herself she had not almost told the truth to a six-year-old.

But Marnie knew. That was the thing Vex learned over the years: Marnie knew. Not the shape of it, not the name, but the fact of it—that her sister carried something in her hands and her chest that did not belong to the Order's neat borders, that the wet cloths and the binding and the careful rituals of hiding were not for a burn scar or an accident. Marnie had the gift of seeing past the story to the truth underneath, and she had looked into Vex's hidden fire and found it not monstrous, not terrifying, but simply *hers*—as much a part of Vex as the flour-dust in her hair or the crescent scars on her palms.

She never said so. But she showed it in a thousand small ways: the way she never flinched when Vex's hands came near the lamp, the way she sat closer to Vex than to anyone else on cold nights by the oven, the way she answered, when their mother asked why she was in the oven room again, "It's warm in here. And Vex is here."

The stories came at night, after the bakery closed and the ovens cooled and the smell of bread lay over the house like a blanket. Marnie would appear in the doorway of Vex's room, tin cup in her hands, blue rim glinting—she always carried that cup to bed, like a blessing, even though she never drank from it at night. She claimed it was for emergencies. The emergency, Vex learned, was boredom.

"Tell me a story. Tell me about the sea."

"There's no sea."

"Tell me about the one that's not there, then."

Vex had never seen the sea. Neither had Marnie. The sea was a heresy, a rumor, a word the Order did not say. But in the dark, with the bakery's warmth settling around them like a second skin, Vex told her sister about it anyway: invented it out of whole cloth, gave it a gray-green color and a smell like salt and old rope, taught her the word *wave* and the word *tide* and the word *horizon*, which Marnie loved because it sounded like a promise.

"It's a place where water falls from the sky," Vex said. "Not rationed. Not measured. It just comes."

"So you'd never be thirsty?"

"You'd never be thirsty."

Marnie was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, in the small fierce voice she used for important things: "When I grow up, I'm going to the sea. You can come."

"I'll come."

"Promise?"

"Promise."

Marnie held out her pinky, the way children do, and Vex hooked her own around it. The small finger was warm and fierce and impossibly alive.

"It's a promise," Marnie said. "You can't unsay it."

No, Vex thought, watching her sister drift toward sleep. Some things you could not unsay once they were said in the world. She had not known then how many things she would say that she could not unsay. She had not known the name of the fire or the shape of the want or the weight of the choice. She had only known that her sister was warm and small and asleep in her lap, and that the world outside the bakery was cold and hungry and waiting.

At the beginning of that last summer—the summer Marnie was eight—the heat lay across the city like a hand. No one said the word *drought* aloud; the Order called it a *trial*, and the Founders called it the natural order of things, and the wells called it what they were: dry. The common well behind the tailor's shop went from sweet to bitter to brackish within a month. The ration lines formed before dawn.

Marnie started coughing in the last week of the summer.

It was a small cough at first, dry, the kind a child gets from dust or from nothing at all. Vex noticed it the way she noticed everything about her sister: with a part of her attention that never quite closed. She noticed the blue-rimmed cup was not being filled as full as it should be. She noticed, with a cold creeping horror she did not name, that her sister's hands trembled when she carried it to bed.

"Marnie. You're coughing."

"It's nothing. I swallowed a fly."

"There are no flies this time of year."

"There's one. He was tiny. He tasted like raisins."

Vex laughed. She always laughed with Marnie, even when the laughter was a mask over the cold thing moving in her chest. She told herself it was the heat. The dry season. It would pass when the rains came.

But the rains did not come.

The cough got worse. It settled into Marnie's chest like something living, a small persistent animal that woke with her and kept her awake at night. Her mother began praying over the dinner table, longer prayers. Vex listened with her head bowed and felt the coal in her chest stir, not with hunger but with something worse: a dawning, sickening fear.

It was the first whisper of the Flux, though no one said the word aloud. On the lower districts, doors began to close at odd hours. A mourning wreath appeared on the door of the basket-weaver's house. Then another. Then another.

Vex held Marnie's hand and told her stories about the sea while her sister coughed and coughed in the darkness of the back room, her blue-rimmed cup empty beside the cot, and she felt the coal in her chest stir with a new hunger: not the bright crackling wanting she had practiced behind the ash pits, but the other kind—the one with eyes. It wanted to correct things. It was patient, and it was deep, and it was growing teeth.

"Marnie," Vex said one night, when the coughing had gone on so long she thought her sister's ribs would break. "I need you to drink."

"There's no more."

"I'll get more."

"Vex." Marnie's voice was thin, but it held the old sharpness, the small queen speaking from her throne of breadcrumb cities. "You can't get what the Founders keep."

The words were not an accusation. They were a fact, stated with the same guileless certainty Marnie had used to pronounce the Order did not own the rats.

And in her chest, the coal cracked open.

"I'll find a way," Vex heard herself say.

Marnie looked at her with the gray-sky eyes that had seen everything from the first moment, and she did not argue. She simply held out her hand, and Vex took it, and the small fingers closed around hers with the same fierce grip they had had on the night of her birth, when Vex had made her first vow.

It had not been enough. None of it had been enough.

In the cell, the drip struck the stone floor with its small, patient sound, and Vex came back to herself with her cheek against the damp wall and the name of her sister a scar in her mouth. The strand of hair was still under her cuff. The block was still loose. The pyre was still being tested above her.

She pressed her palms flat against the stone, feeling the crescents cool and quiet, and said it aloud, the way she had said it every night since the fire:

"Hello, Marnie. I'm still your sister. I'm still sorry."

Above her, the sounds of the city went on: cart wheels, distant voices, a child's laugh, bright and careless, running across the square like a stone skipped over water. It was the same laugh she had heard a hundred times in the bakery, in the oven room, in the dark when the stories ran low and the sea rose up to meet them. It ran on without her, bright and careless, and Vex held her sister's name in her mouth like a coal that would not cool.

chapters.name: The Service Gate
chapters.content:
The hammering stopped the way it had stopped before: not with a last nail but with a silence that came down over the square like a lid. Vex lay in the dark of the tear-shaped cell and listened to that silence settle. It had a shape. It was the shape of a pyre standing where the market had stood, its wood tested, its corners true, waiting for a body.

The tunnel breathed against her wrist. She had left the block loose, a dark mouth in the wall; no voice had come through it since the voice that said *I'll come back*, and had not come back. She had not sealed it. She had not decided whether sealing it was hope or fear, and so she had done neither, and listened to the drip make its slow coin-sound against the stone, and waited.

She had known a door once. Not a door in a wall—a door in a gate, cut for hands and small things, a small door inside a large one. She had stood on one side of it for a season and learned what it meant to wait. The knowledge had come back to her in the night, the way the dead come back: not walking, not speaking, but standing where they had always stood, patient as a question.

The service gate of the Founders' Quarter. And the man who kept it.

"Corin," she said to the dark. The name came out hoarse. She had not said it aloud in years.

The first time she went to the service gate, she went for water. That was the thing to remember. Not for bread, not for scraps. The common well behind the tailor's shop had gone brackish, the north cistern was rationed, and her mother's jars stood empty on the shelf like a row of small open mouths. There was water inside the Founders' Quarter. Everyone knew this. The Founders' fountain ran day and night for the sound of it, and the horses drank from a trough that was never allowed to run dry, and the kitchens washed their dishes in water so clean and plentiful that the poor carried the memory of its taste in their mouths like a shame.

The service gate was nothing like the high gates that opened for the Founders' carriages. It was a narrow iron mouth in the wall's shoulder, rust-flaking, hung with a bell that no one rang. Set into it was the wicket: a small door cut for hands and small things, no higher than her chest, barred with iron. Vex had stood before it a long time that first day, her empty jar in her hand, listening to the fountain on the other side of the wall, letting the sound of all that wasted water do its work on her resolve. The fountain ran and ran. It did not stop. It did not ask whose child was thirsty.

The gate had a liturgy. The poor who came were not a mob but a congregation, and the gate had rules older than she was. The one-armed carter stood nearest the wicket because a Founders' grain cart had taken his arm and a Founders' clerk had paid him off in lentils, and the lentils were gone but his place was not. The woman with the baby stood second, because of the baby. The old stonemason stood third because he was old and had set the stones of the wall himself, before the glass was set along the top. There were others. There were always others. The gate did not punish those who waited. It punished those who pushed, and it had a quantity of punishment to spare, laid at the feet of one man.

Corin.

She saw him that first day, on the far side of the iron, and did not yet know his name. He was a uniform to her: the Founders' blue, worn thin at the elbows, a belt notched a hole past comfortable, a truncheon carried like a walking stick rather than a weapon. His face was the kind that had been open before the city closed it—broad, tired, creased around the mouth as if he had spent years not saying things. He looked at Vex with the flat assessment of a man who has learned to spot trouble the way other men spot weather, and he looked past her, and the wicket stayed shut.

The kitchens' bucket came a bell later. A scullion shoved it through the wicket, and Corin took possession of it as if the bucket were the gate and he its only true keeper. He did not open the gate. The gate never opened for the poor, not that whole season, not once. The bread, the potatoes, the occasional crooked jug of water came through the small door, and the small door was enough to keep the large one shut. That was the trick of it. Vex was young, but not so young she could not see where the trick sat in the machinery.

"Marta." The woman with the baby stepped forward, folded the heel and the soft-eyed potatoes into her apron, and stood aside.

"Bas."

"Tam."

"New girl."

Vex startled. Up the line, the one-armed carter looked at her with something like pity for her ignorance. She walked to the wicket, and Corin held out a heel of bread—gray, hard, a whole heel, more than the bakery's scraps gave her in a day—and said, "Don't make trouble."

She took the bread and stood too long holding it, because she did not know that the custom was to take what you were given and go. Corin looked at her over the wicket's iron rail.

"That's the price of this gate," he said. "Don't make trouble. Don't crowd the door. Don't come in a group. Come alone, come quiet, take what you're given, and go. Do that, and I don't see you. Do anything else, and I see you, and I close the wicket, and the congregation will know it was your fault."

"I understand," she said.

He waited. Her feet did not move.

"You want the water," he said.

She had not realized her jar was so loud—a clay pot, corked, hung from a cord. She had wanted to be invisible and had brought her hunger to the gate wearing it around her wrist.

Corin looked over his shoulder into the yard, where the Founders' horses' trough stood against the wall, iron-bound, fed by a pipe that ran when the stable lads remembered to turn it. He took the jar from her hand and walked to the trough with the particular stillness of a man doing a small dangerous thing—not furtive; too old for furtive, but set, shoulders ready, eyes on the doorways. He filled the jar to the neck, corked it, came back, and passed it through the wicket.

"Tell no one," he said.

She put the jar against her chest. The water was cold through the clay, colder than anything her hands had held in months. It smelled of horse and leather and cut grass.

"Thank you," she said.

He had already turned away. He had already closed his eyes to her, which was the only way he could be kind.

She carried the water home like a stolen host. Marnie sat at the table with her blue-rimmed cup in front of her, and Vex poured out a palm's depth, and Marnie drank it slowly, the way she had been taught to drink anything precious, and said, "It tastes like grass."

"It's the Founders' water," Vex said.

Marnie's gray-sky eyes went through a calculation Vex could not follow and came out somewhere safe. "Then it's stolen," Marnie said, with no judgment at all, and drank the rest.

Their mother said nothing about the jar, nothing about the water. She looked at Vex with the particular stillness of a woman who has recognized a thing and chosen not to name it. The wanting under Vex's ribs, the coal under ash, turned its slow eye to the sound of the water going down her sister's throat and said nothing at all.

She went back. Three days a week at first, then five, then every day the gate was open. She learned the liturgy. She learned that Corin never handed her the bread after that first day—he left it: on the sill of the wicket, on the stone by her foot, weighted with a scrap of sacking so the wind could not take it. It appeared as she turned to go, like something that had always been there. When she thanked him he looked at the wall, not at her. He was giving her nothing. A blind man cannot bear witness. A gate that does not see you cannot be held accountable.

That was the arrangement. They did not speak of it. He told her once that she looked the way his sister had at fourteen—sharp, watchful, hands always a little too still—and then he told her to forget he had said that, and neither of them mentioned it again.

The wanting grew teeth in that season, at that gate. Not the crackling kind she fed behind the ash pits, the bright kind that answered to her will. The other kind: the slow one with eyes, the corrector, the coal that had found its injustice at the public board and the water law and the menu nailed up beside the ration notices. Standing in the line of the permanent poor, watching a blue coat come down the lane, Vex felt the coal turn, and knew that the fire in her hands was not the only thing she had hidden from her mother. She had hidden a whole arithmetic, and the arithmetic had a conclusion it was waiting to draw.

The steward came on a day when the congregation had grown. A new family had come from the tanners' row—a father with a child on his hip, and the child was crying because it was thirsty, the way children cry for thirst, a sound that stops the heart and then stops meaning anything because it does not stop. The father was crying without tears, because tears are water too, and water was what he did not have.

Corin was going down the line with the bucket when the steward came through the high gate, not the service gate: a coat of deep blue wool that cost more than the houses on Vex's lane, a chain of office, a face like a door.

The line went quiet. Not respect: the particular silence of animals who have learned not to draw attention to the bones they are hiding.

The steward looked at the line. He looked at Corin, who had straightened in one breath into a different man—spine locked, face empty, a man who was no one's brother and no one's blind eye.

"I've told you about feeding the vermin," the steward said.

"Yes, sir," said Corin.

"This is not a soup kitchen. It is the service gate of the Founders' Quarter."

"Yes, sir."

"They breed, you know. You feed them, they breed."

Corin said nothing.

The steward walked to the bucket and kicked it over with one polished boot. The bread rolled in the dust. The potatoes went into the gutter. The father made a sound that was not quite a word.

Corin stood at attention and looked at nothing.

The steward left.

For a long moment no one moved. Then Corin picked up the bucket, set it upright, walked down the line, picked the bread out of the dust, brushed it with his thumb, and gave it to the father, whose hands were shaking. Then he went to the wicket.

"That's all," he said. "Come back tomorrow."

The congregation dispersed. Vex did not. When the lane was empty, Corin looked at her over the iron rail, and his face was no longer empty. It was the face of a man who has been kicked and cannot kick back and has been saying *yes, sir* for so long he has forgotten whether he owns a no.

"That's the trick of it, girl," he said, to the iron, not to her. "You stand where the water runs, and you don't get wet. Stand here long enough, you think you're dry. You're not. You're just under the roof of the house that owns the rain."

She began to understand, in that season, Meridian's true arithmetic. The Founders did not need to be cruel. They had hired a thousand Corins—men who hated the orders they obeyed, who let the scraps leak and kept the gate shut. The bread was the price of the gate. Enough mercy to make the waiting bearable, enough waiting to make the gate necessary. A man who is fed just enough does not test the lock. A city fed just enough does not burn.

Corin was the middleman of the tyranny. He did not own the cisterns. He had never signed an order. But he stood between the thirsty and the water, and his own bread was in his mouth, and his sister was in the wash-house, and every kindness he committed was a kindness the system had already priced. Vex saw all of this, and she loved him anyway—if love is the word for the ache you feel for someone who is doing all he can and it will never be enough. She loved him the way she loved the seamstress who sold her ring for a bucket of bad water. She loved him the way you love the wounded. It did not make her want the fire less. It made her want it differently: not hot but cold, the way a key is cold, the way a verdict is cold.

Once, she saw the sister. Laundry day, the wash-house door open, steam rolling out into the yard, and a woman came across the cobbles with a basket heaped with linen—sunbonnet, sleeves rolled past the elbow, a way of walking that was Corin's way, shoulders set, looking at no one. Vex did not speak. The woman did not look at her.

"She doesn't know," Corin said from the gate. "About the bread. About the water. She thinks I'm a hard man." He laughed, a bare stone dropped into a dry well. "I let her think it. It's the only thing I've ever given her worth keeping."

Vex never learned the sister's name.

She stopped coming when the bread stopped mattering. That was the way it ended—not with a word, not with a quarrel. Marnie began to cough that autumn, a small dry cough at first, the sound of dust breathed off a dry shelf, and the heel of bread that had been a marvel the summer before was a marvel no longer. The bread could not sit by Marnie's bed. The water could not unblue her lips. The gate, for all its small mercies, had nothing that could hold her sister still in the world.

She had meant to go back and say thank you. She had meant to tell Corin what the water had meant, the cold of it through the clay, the grass-smell of it going down Marnie's throat. She had meant to be grateful the way a person owes gratitude—in full, in kind, in public.

The fire had made other plans. The fire had burned the wash-house where the sister worked. The fire had burned the service gate, and the wicket, and the bucket, and the arithmetic.

In the cell, the memory folded away from her like a page turning. The damp wall was against her cheek. The tunnel breathed at her wrist. Above, the pyre stood in the square, and she could hear the festival quiet of a city that had made of her death a holiday.

She had looked for Corin once, at the trial. From behind the gag, she had searched the gallery for the heavy-shouldered man with the tired face—to ask him, with her eyes, whether he had been at the gate when the fire came, whether he had seen the wash-house go, whether he knew which of the ledgers held his sister's name. She had not found him. She did not know if he had been off duty. She did not know if he had watched her walk to the pyre and felt the small door inside him close at last.

The guard who brought her bread now had the same tired kindness, the same refusal to be fully cruel, the same share of complicity. Corin was everywhere in this city. He was the country she had lived in all her life: the good man who cannot open the gate.

The loose block lay against her thigh. A door in a wall, where the service gate had been a door within a door. A hand had reached through the dark and spoken her name. She had not decided whether that hand was another Corin—kind, afraid, rationing mercy to keep the waiting bearable—or something that wanted what the fire could do. She had not decided whether there was a difference.

"Corin," she said again, to the stone, to the dark, to the face she had never seen again. "I couldn't save her. I couldn't save any of them."

No answer came. Above, the Sanctum bell struck the hour, steady and without malice. The pyre waited in the square. It had no wicket, no guard to turn a blind eye, no bread slipped through a small door, no small mercy to make the waiting bearable. It was the only door in Meridian that would open for her.

chapters.name: Thistle's Eyes
chapters.content:
The service gate had another face. It was not Corin's.

Vex lay on the stone of the tear-shaped cell with the pyre's finished silence pressed over her like a lid, and the memory came the way the dead come back — not walking, not speaking, but standing where they had always stood. The gate had two doors in it that summer: the wicket, and the fact of the girl who used it.

She had been coming to the service gate for three weeks before she saw the face. The scraps arrived the way they always arrived — a hand, a wrist, a basket shoved through the wicket into the light, and gone. Scullions did not show their faces at the gate. That was the first law of the service gate, older than the Order, older than the Founders: the bread is there, the water is there, the face is not. A gift that can be seen can be named. A gift that cannot be named cannot be taken from you for eating it.

Then one afternoon the hand did not withdraw.

Vex looked up from the bread — gray, hard, still warm from the kitchen — and met the eyes. Gray-green. Not the gray of the common well gone bitter, not the green of the moss on the Founders' wall. The color of water that does not ask permission, water that has never been counted out into anyone's cup, water that moves. Vex did not know the word for what she was seeing. She only knew it did not belong to Meridian, and that it was looking at her with a candor the city had beaten out of everyone she knew.

The face around the eyes was sharp-chinned and small, younger than Vex by a year or two. A cap failed against a chaos of dark hair. The eyes had too much in them for the face — they had seen the inside of the Founders' kitchen, the steward's mouth, the cold arithmetic of the pantry, and they had not learned to hide it.

"Huh," the girl said.

It was not a word. It was an appraisal, and it went all the way down.

Vex said nothing. She had learned to let the gate do the talking.

The girl's mouth twitched. Then she laughed — sharp, crooked, quick, a stone skipped across water. It was not a kind laugh and not an unkind one. It was a laugh that had seen the joke from both sides and found it funny anyway, with the corners still frayed.

"Don't tell them," she said, and tipped the heel of bread through the wicket. Warm. Flour-dusted. "And don't make me sorry."

The bread settled into Vex's hands, and the warmth of it went through her like a small betrayal — a burning sun in her palms, the heat's echo, the thing she buried behind the ash pits stirring in its sleep. She closed her fingers over the crust and held the fire under, hard, the way she had held it every day for years. It obeyed. It always obeyed, when she gripped it early.

"You're the one who comes for water," the girl said. "The baker's girl. Corin told me."

"You oughtn't to tell people about the gate."

"Corin keeps his mouth the way the Order keeps holy relics. I'm better." The chin went up, a stubborn chin that had already made its decision about her. "I'm Thistle."

It was not a Founders' name. It was a lower-district word for something that grew where no one had planted it and bit when you tried to pull it up. Vex liked it. She did not know yet how much she would come to like it — that one day she would say it aloud in a tear-shaped cell, and the stone would not answer.

"I'm Vex."

"I know." Thistle's head cocked. There was a flicker in the gray-green eyes, not calculation — recognition. "You look the way I'd look if I'd been keeping a secret too long."

Vex went still.

"It's not hard to see," Thistle said. "You hold yourself like someone who's afraid of being seen and can't quite manage to hide it. I know the feeling. I just don't have the choice. The wicket's all there is of me that fits through this gate." She grinned — quick, crooked, gone. "Come back tomorrow. I'll have something worth the walk."

She did.

Thistle was not at the wicket every day — the kitchen had a rhythm, and the wicket was one small task in a long day of tasks — but when she was, she left the scrap basket open a moment longer and let the talk run through the small door with the bread. Vex brought the news of the lower districts, the life the Founders' Quarter never saw: the common well gone bitter, the ration line around the corner of the rag market, the water law board's new schedule nailed up beside the Founders' menu. Thistle listened with her chin in her hands, hungry for it, and fed it back as mockery.

She was a mimic. It was her one permitted rebellion, and she worked at it with a craftsman's care. Founders all had the same walk, she said — the chest first, the head last, the feet as if they were being lowered into holy water — and she could do all of them. She did the steward's sermon on providence in a voice of warm honey poured over stones: "And in their great mercy, the keepers of the water have seen fit to keep it." She did the Bishop's walk around the censer. She did a Founder tasting the cream served in cups of cistern ice, holding the cup at arm's length as if it were the Host.

The first time Vex laughed, it came out too loud, and she clamped a hand over her mouth and looked for the watch. Thistle's eyes brightened. By the third afternoon, Vex was laughing until her ribs hurt, snorting, wiping her eyes on a wrist that still carried flour. It was the most alive she had ever felt. In the bakery, laughter was a currency you spent carefully. At the wicket, it grew on the air, free, and no one measured it out.

But under the mockery there was a blade, and one day Thistle laid it on the sill.

They had been naming the Founders' sins — a litany the way children learn cruel rhymes for cruel adults: the locked cisterns, the fountain that ran day and night for the sound of it, the banquet menus posted beside the ration notices. Vex was laughing at her own addition when Thistle went quiet.

"They think we're patient," Thistle said. The mimic's voice was gone; this was the voice under it, the one from the bottom of the well. "They think we're grateful. They think the Order is right — that suffering is a test, and that we pass it by dying quietly." She looked at Vex, and the gray-green eyes were the color of deep water. "I'd like to see the Founders feel it. Just once. Just one day of the ration line. One hour watching their children's lips go blue."

The heat stirred in Vex's chest, rose like a hand reaching for the sill, and she caught it, held it down, pressed it back into the coal under ash. She could not tell Thistle what lived in her hands. She could not tell anyone. But she could feel the shape of the wanting — how close it stood to Thistle's wanting, two people leaning so far toward each other they had become a single shadow.

"I like your laugh," Vex said. It was not the answer. It was the only true thing she could say.

Thistle looked at her a long moment. Then the laugh came back, crooked and quick, and the blade was put away. But Vex had seen it. She would remember exactly where it was kept.

She told Thistle nothing of the fire. That was a rule with iron in it, sealed with wet cloths and her mother's fear. She learned to take the scraps from Thistle without touching her, to keep her palms turned inward when she laughed, to fold her arms so the crescent scars stayed hidden in the folds of her sleeves. She thought she had made them invisible.

But Thistle had eyes that had learned to read what people did not say — the kitchen was a school, and the steward was a cruel teacher.

One day, watching Vex fold her hands in her lap, Thistle said, "What do you keep in your palms?"

It was close enough to the truth that the heat jumped in Vex's chest. She made herself breathe. "Flour. Like everyone. I'm a baker."

"No." Thistle was not smiling. "I mean it truly. You hide them like they're worth something. Like they're dangerous." Her head tilted. "Are they?"

The silence stretched. A cart passed in the street; a bird argued with the bakery's cat. Vex could feel the heat waiting under her ribs, answering the question with a truth Thistle could not see.

"Everyone's dangerous," Vex said carefully, "if you push them to the gate."

Thistle studied her. Then she grinned — the real one, the one that showed the girl underneath the cap and the blade. "Good," she said. "I like danger. I like that you're hiding it." She leaned close to the wicket, and her voice dropped to a conspirator's whisper. "You're the most interesting thing that has ever fit through this gate. Don't make me sorry you did."

The curfew had a loophole in it if you knew where to stand. It came by districts, and the lane behind the fish-monger's sat at the seam of two of them, so each watchman assumed the other had cleared it. Vex had known the loophole for a year. She had never used it — until Thistle, with the gate shut behind her at dusk, mouthed through the iron: "The lane behind the fish-monger's. After the bell. Bring something warm."

Vex stole her mother's blanket from the trunk — the good wool one, the one her mother had carried out of her own childhood — and slipped into the dark the way the wanting had taught her: soft, flat, nothing to see. The lane was a slit of cobbles and old scales. Thistle was waiting on the back steps, wrapped in a sacking apron that barely reached her ankles, her cap off at last. Her hair went everywhere.

"You came," Thistle said. It was almost surprised.

"You said to."

"People say things through gates they don't mean when the gate is shut."

"I'm not people," Vex said, "and I'm not through the gate."

They sat on the steps, wrapped in two kinds of wool, and the city settled around them — the fish-monger's shutters, the bell-tower's slow breathing, the curfew's silence settling like dust. The lantern in the fish-monger's yard burned a rationed flame in its iron cage. Above, the sky was the color of the inside of a cup.

Thistle talked about the sea.

It had come to her by accident — a book left open on the steward's desk, a page she had been forbidden to touch and had touched anyway while scrubbing the floor around it. A picture: gray water to the far edge of the world, no shore at the edge, just more water, and a word under it she had sounded out letter by letter with the steward's boots coming down the corridor. The sea. Meridian had no sea. The sea was a rumor, a heresy, a word the Order did not say — because water that did not come from the cisterns was water that did not answer to the keepers, and the Chastened Flame had no prayer for it.

"It moves," Thistle said. The mockery, the blade, the quick crooked joking — all gone. This was the voice under the voice, and she gave it to Vex in the dark like the heel of bread, with both hands. "All the time. It does not stop. It does not ask permission. It does not wait for the steward to unlock anything."

In the sea, Thistle said, water fell from the sky. Not rationed. Not measured. It just came — the sky opened and gave it, the way a mother gives bread to a child without weighing it. Everyone drank. No one asked whose name was on the cistern, because there was no cistern. There was only the water and the sky, and the sky had never once closed its gate.

"I'm going to see it someday." The words were small, and they were the largest thing Vex had ever heard spoken — a door opened in the middle of the dark. "I'm going to stand at the edge and put my hands in it, and it will be warm, and it will not be counted out to me." Her voice caught. She swallowed, and went on. "I'm going to see the sea. And I'm going to laugh. And no one is going to tell me to be quiet."

The night did not answer. The lantern guttered in its cage. The bell-tower had finished breathing.

Vex thought: *I will go with you. I will keep you safe. I will burn anything that tries to stop you.* She did not say it. The fire was a door she had never opened in front of anyone, and she knew, even then, that it was not a small thing — it was a hunger with teeth, and if she ever opened it, it would not be a candle she could cup in her hands.

Thistle looked at her. "What are you staring at?"

"The sea," Vex said.

Thistle laughed — the real laugh, quick and crooked — and Vex reached across the blanket and took her hand. The fingers were cold, callused, small, and they curled around hers like they had been waiting for the offer.

"You're warm," Thistle said. "Why are you so warm?"

The heat under Vex's skin answered — rising, reaching. She forced it down and squeezed Thistle's hand instead of letting the fire answer for her.

"I'm a baker. I work near the oven."

Thistle held her gaze a moment longer — the eyes too old, the sea in them, reading the door Vex had not opened. Then she smiled, quick and crooked and defiant, a small warm thing in a city full of locked cisterns.

It is the last time Vex sees her whole.

The memory folded shut like the wicket closing. The cell came back: the drip, the shaft of light, the pyre's silence overhead. Vex lay with her cheek against the stone and felt the boundary between the memory and the loss — the broken place where the gate had been, the lane behind the fish-monger's, the crooked grin gone to ash in the first heat of a fire Thistle had never asked for.

She had wanted the Founders to feel it just once, Vex thought. One day of the ration line. One hour watching their children's lips go blue. And Vex — who could not tell her what lived in her hands, who had let her be drawn to a danger she sensed but could not name — had given her the opposite of what she asked. Not one hour. Not one day. An inferno. No arithmetic in the world would balance that account.

Thistle never saw the sea. The sea was the one gate that had always stood open — no wicket, no guard, no measured water — and Vex's hands had closed it.

She said the name aloud to the stone, the way she had said it a hundred times in this cell. "Thistle."

The drip answered. The silence lied, saying nothing had ever burned.

But under her cuff, the strand of dark hair — not Thistle's; a different dark, a different door — caught the light like a thread of something Vex had not yet named. Someone had dug toward her through the dark. Someone had asked if she was alive. Vex did not know if the hand reaching for her wanted the fire or wanted the woman. She did not know if there was a difference.

She tucked the strand deeper into her sleeve and lay in the dark of the tear-shaped cell with the dead beside her: a sister, a scullery maid, a child in a white dress — and the sea they would never see, gray-green, moving, asking no one's permission.

chapters.name: The Banquet Menu
chapters.content:
The drip measured the cell the way a cup measures hunger: one drop, one hour, one more name for the dead. Vex lay still in the dark and let the last summer come. It came the way the tunnel had come—one stone at a time, patient, sure of what it would find. Heat like a hand flat on the nape of the city's neck. The wells going dry. Marnie's cough beginning like a crack in a cup. And the menu, pinned over the ration board like a flag planted on conquered ground.

The public board stood where Ash Lane met the Long Market, walled three deep in notices. Ration schedules. Water law under the Founders' seal—WE GUARD WHAT WE HOLD. A ledger page, the lower districts' column crossed out in iron-red ink: *closed until rains.* And over all of it, pinned like a banner, the Founders' menu for the Feast of the Chaste Flame.

Cream paper. Gold ink. A border of painted waves, for the Feast—the sea drawn in blue along the edge, the sea the lower districts had never seen, mocked by the Founders' own hand. A reader was sounding it out for the ration line, the way the Order read scripture:

"First, oysters from the coast, on ice."

A child in the crowd: "What's ice?"

"Second, quail in honey, glazed until it shines. Third, wine-glazed pheasant."

"Fourth," the reader said, and his voice cracked, "a cream served in cups of cistern ice."

The ration line went quiet. The reader went on—boar, a tower of spun sugar, marzipan in the shape of the Founders' fountain—but no one was listening anymore. Someone laughed, a dry well of a laugh with nothing at the bottom. "Cups of cistern ice," a woman said. "The Founders will eat the cistern itself, and we'll be drinking chalk and calling it providence."

"Seven courses," an old man said, counting on his fingers. "Seven buckets between the two streets in a week, and two of those went to the woman with the baby. You tell me which ledger the Chaste Flame is keeping."

Vex read the menu herself, word by word, and the coal under ash broke open and showed its eyes.

Years she had watched them. The water tax tripling. The carts rolling past the poor districts without stopping. The fountain in the Founders' Quarter running day and night for the sound of it. She had called it cruelty, and cruelty was a door she could stand in front of and hate. This was different. The menu did not threaten; it did not gloat; it did not even see her. It was simply the sentence the cistern had always written, printed on cream paper, while the city's other half measured out its life in buckets.

Thistle's voice came through the wicket of memory, sharp as ever: *I'd like to see the Founders feel it. Just once. Just one day of the ration line. One hour watching their children's lips go blue.*

Vex had laughed at that once. She did not laugh now. The coal's eyes were open, and they were hers.

She turned from the board and ran.

The bakery was wrong before she was through the door. The ovens were banked. The air had the closed-in smell of sickness, which borrows its odor from everything it touches. Her mother stood at the foot of the cot in the back room holding a cloth that was dry for the lack of water to wet it. Her face had the look of a door that has been knocked on too long.

Marnie lay with her gray eyes half open—the color of the sky before rain, and no rain in them. Heat came off her skin like a banked oven. Her lips were the blue of the rim of her tin cup. The cup stood on the floor beside the cot, empty, its blue rim the one true thing in the room.

"Vex." Marnie's voice was a scrape of dry leaves. "Tell me the sea."

"The sea," Vex said. "Gray-green. Moving. Water falls from the sky there, not rationed, not measured—" She could not finish. The story could not fill a cup.

Her mother said, "I gave her my share. There's nothing left until the cart."

"The cart won't come."

"Vex—"

But she was already through the door, the coal burning its way up her throat.

The healer's door was shutting for dusk. Vex caught it at the last hand's breadth, her palm flat to the wood, and the bolt stopped a finger from the latch.

"Please," she said. "My sister. She's eight. She has the fever—"

"Householders first, paid by the quarter." The voice came through the gap, tired as old linen. "Come back at first bell."

"She'll be dead by first bell."

"Then she will be with the Chaste Flame, and you will not have to watch." The bolt slid home.

The water-seller's cart stood at the lane's end. A woman was taking her bucket—short measure, everyone saw the two fingers of air and said nothing, because to speak was to lose the bucket. Vex put herself in front of the horse.

"My sister needs water. Just a cup."

"Proof of residence. Ration book. Fee."

"I don't have a fee."

"Then the Order will test her, and she will pass the test the way we all pass it." He nodded at the bay horse, glossy, sleek, better fed than any child on the lane. It drank and did not look at her. "You want what's in that trough, you talk to the Founder who owns it."

She ran.

The north cistern was locked. It had always been locked; the chain was new in her childhood and still new, because the Founders' locks did not rust without permission. The guard there was a man like Corin—the good man who cannot open the gate. He looked at her empty jar and did the arithmetic and said, "I can't, girl."

"Your fountain runs for the sound of it," Vex said. "Day and night. One bucket."

"Go home," he said, gently, and his hand lay on the key at his belt and did not move.

The common well at the fish-monger's rose with the bucket full of nothing—wet rope, iron taste, a mouth with the tongue taken out.

She passed the service gate. The wicket was closed. She did not stop. The bread could not sit by Marnie's bed; the bread had never once stopped a cough. But she thought of Thistle inside those walls, scrubbing a pan that had held the quail in honey, while the cream cooled in cups of cistern ice. Thistle's dream was a book left open on the steward's desk: the sea, water that falls from the sky, that does not ask permission, that has never once closed its gate. The Founders ate the sea's harvest—first course, oysters from the coast, on ice—and the sea, the one gate that had always stood open, might as well have been a locked cistern between them.

Vex went home with the empty jar.

Dusk. The Order's bell. Her mother had found half a cup somewhere—Vex never learned where—and Marnie had drunk it, and it had barely wet the blue of her lips. The cup stood empty again. The blue rim was a small proclamation.

Marnie's hand found Vex's wrist. The grip was weaker than it had been at her birth, weaker than the pinky promise, but it held.

"We're still going to the sea," Marnie said. Not a question. The fiercest thing Vex had ever heard an eight-year-old say, and it broke her in half.

"Yes," Vex said. "We're still going."

"You can't unsay it."

"I won't unsay it."

Marnie smiled, the first smile in three days, and let go, and slept.

Vex sat in the lamplight and let the coal take shape.

She had spent her life promising to aim it. Gates, not people. Ledgers, not the hands that wrote them. She had practiced behind the ash pits, fire answering to wanting, wanting answering to will. And now the wanting had a shape at last, and the shape was not gates. It was a cup with a blue rim, held up to the last of the light by a child who believed her sister could find water in a dry city.

The Founders were not merely cruel. Cruelty was human; cruelty could be reasoned with, outlived, forgiven. This was a machine. It measured water in cups and called the measurement order. It posted a seven-course menu beside a ration schedule and called the contrast providence. It paid the Order to bless the machine and the law to write it down and the good men to guard it—Corin, the cistern guard, the water-seller with his horse—each paid just enough to believe it was not their hands turning the wheel.

A disease. Not a faction, not a family, not even the Founders themselves. A disease built into the city like a cistern, and the disease wore the city's own face.

And something inside her knew how to cauterize.

She looked at her palms. The twin crescents, pale in the lamplight, there since before memory. The Order called them the mark of the Unmaking. Her mother called them an oven-paddle scar. Vex had never known what to call them.

Now she knew. They were the mouth of the thing inside her. And the thing was not a candle and not a hunger—it was a physician. It knew rot when it saw it. It knew what to cut away.

Not Marnie. Not Thistle. Not the laundress, not the seamstress, not the children. The disease.

She had promised behind the ash pits never to burn anything living again, and she had buried the beetle's shell under a stone and meant it. She meant it still. She would aim it so carefully. Gates. Locks. Ledgers. The menu. The key. The cup of cistern ice. The Founders would feel one day of the ration line—one hour of blue lips. Thistle's wish. Marnie's thirst. All of it, corrected.

She told herself she was in control.

She told herself the fire knew her voice.

She told herself the ledgers had no faces.

And somewhere in the Founders' Quarter the feast began. The music floated over the wall—strings and a flute, light, gloating—the same music that had floated over the walls all summer while the wells shrank and the healer's door stayed shut. Marnie stirred and coughed, a dry ratchet of a sound, and did not wake.

Vex sat with her palms open, the crescents catching the lamplight, and felt the coal settle into a shape that would not unmake itself.

A choice was a thing you could not unsay. Loaves on a shelf. She had known it since the flour-fire behind the ash pits.

She was still sitting there when the music stopped and the far bell tolled the hour, and she knew, the way you know the shape of your own hand, what she would do once her mother had gone to bed.

The memory folded shut like the service gate closing.

Vex came back to herself in the oubliette: the drip, the dark, her hands flat against the cold stone. The coal was still there—it had never left. It burned patient as a key in a lock, and the heat coiled under her palms.

The disease had worn her face instead. It had worn Thistle's smile, Marnie's cup, the Foundling child's white dress. Fire did not know the difference between a ledger and a face, and she had known it could not know. She had told herself she was in control. She had uncurled her fingers anyway.

Behind the wall, the stone shifted—one, then two, then a pause, then one.

Vex did not answer. She pressed her palms flat to the rock and let the heat bleed into it, and the coal burned steady, waiting for the pyre. She had never learned to control the fire. She had only learned to want the right thing burned, and the city's answer had been to take her wanting, name it heresy, and build a pyre for it. At the trial, no one mentioned the menu. No one mentioned the blue-rimmed cup. The city had burned the pages it did not want to read and called the ash justice.

The menu was still pinned behind her eyes: cream in cups of cistern ice, and a girl holding up an empty cup with a blue rim, waiting for her sister to find water in a dry city. Vex touched the strand of hair under her cuff—a different dark, a different door—and did not take it out.

Between the tunnel and the pyre she sat, with the coal and the cup and the menu, and the drip measured the dark.

chapters.name: The Night of the Wake
chapters.content:
The drip said her name. Marnie. The shaft of light had gone out; the Sanctum bell was silent; the cell was dark as the bottom of the dry well. Vex lay on the stone with her palms open and let the memory take her under.

The Flux moved through the lower districts not like a wave but like a rumor that passed from door to door, and left a black ribbon on every door it visited. First the coughing—the dry ratchet that began at night and did not stop—then the blue lips, then the wreaths. By the third week every lane had its ribbon, and the dead-cart came at dusk, and the Order's priest stood over the pile of the dead and said a prayer that sounded less like a prayer than a receipt: they had passed the test, they were with the Chaste Flame, the living could stop weeping now and go back to work.

The Founders' healers served the rich. That was what the Order called order. At first bell the healer's door stood open a hand's breadth, and the poor made a line that reached the corner, and a servant read from a card and turned them away one by one: householders first, paid by the quarter, no alms without proof of residence. A Founder's daughter came up the lane in a litter, pale and wrapped in fur, and the door opened the full width for her and closed again, and the line stood looking at the closed door and did not move. The law was on the side of the owners of water. It had always been. Vex had known it since the summer she watched a seamstress trade her wedding ring for a bucket of brackish water. Knowing it in her bones had never once opened a gate.

She ran. That was all she could do—run. To the water-seller's cart, where the price had doubled overnight and the bay horse stood drinking from a full trough, better fed than any child on the lane. To the north cistern, where the guard she had begged the night before stood with his hand on the key and did not move: "I can't, girl." To the common well, where the bucket came up full of mud, a mouth with the tongue taken out. She begged the water-seller for credit; he said the price was two now, come back tomorrow. The seamstress, who had no ring left, gave her a heel of bread and a dipper from the water she had measured out for her own children. Corin's gate she did not go to. The bread could not sit by Marnie's bed.

It was a Founders' water cart that made her a thief. It stood outside a shuttered house, the carter gone in for his coin, the canvas cover tied over the barrel. Vex looked at the shuttered house and the sleeping horse and the barrel that belonged to no one she could name, and she thought of the blue-rimmed cup on the floor beside her sister's cot, and she went around to the back, untied the rope, and filled the clay jar from the tap. The water was cold. It was not hers. She ran with the jar hugged to her chest like a stolen heart, and the stitch in her side was a second breath, and she did not care.

Her mother stood at the foot of the cot. The room had the closed-in smell of sickness, but that was not what was wrong. What was wrong was the quiet. Marnie's cough had stopped.

The fever had taken her past coughing. She lay with her eyes half open, the gray-sky eyes, her lips the blue of the rim of her cup, and her breath came in small rattles, the last water finding the bottom of a dry well. Vex knelt. She unstoppered the stolen jar and put it to her sister's lips. Some of the water went in; some ran down her chin; Marnie did not open her eyes. Vex called her name. The small hand found her wrist, weaker than the pinky promise, but it held.

"Tell me the sea."

Vex told her. The gray-green water, the moving, the water that fell from the sky not rationed not measured, the warm sand, the boat with a white sail sewn from the flour sacks.
